Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to create continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated. We introduce a memory-efficient technique to extend contiguous sequences through nodes with two or more edges, facilitating genome assembly. From a computational complexity perspective, the proposed approach has a $O(\log N)$ overhead and can be efficiently scaled using $P$ processors. Experimental results on a 64-node cluster demonstrate the assembly of a 200-MB wheat genome in under 20 minutes with minimal fragmentation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability to assemble entire chromosomes within a single node with 64 GB RAM by employing our proposed strategy. This marks a significant advancement, outperforming existing approaches by enabling the construction of much longer contiguous sequences. Evaluations using 34 large genomes reveal an average 1.4-fold to 4.3-fold increase in contiguous sequence length compared to existing methods. The proposed approach boasts improved scalability and efficacy compared to other state-of-the-art assembly methods. The code for this research is openly available on the GitHub platform. The proposed algorithm is designated as HiAsiaOx and is designed for assembling plants, but is also compatible with other organisms. This foundation will likely lead to further development and refinement to make HiAsiaOx a more general-purpose assembly tool. Instead, we are exploring a more unified assembly strategy, HiAsiaOx2, to broaden its applicability to a wider range of organisms. This will involve HiAsiaOx2's ability to assemble contigs across different chromosomal regions and incorporate additional oxido-reduction pathways. This will be facilitated through the integration of HiAsiaOx2's graph abstraction and sparse matrix contig creation with existing bi-directional assembly strategies. This will notably involve the utilization of HiAsiaOx2's abridged graph and sparse matrices to enhance its performance and scalability. This will be achieved through the employment of a novel, distributed memory parallel approach for in-graph contig creation. This will notably involve the extension of existing in-graph assembly strategies to scale with multiple processors. The concept of statistical depth has the potential to be used extensively for measuring the hierarchical ranking of both multivariate sufficient statistics and functional data, but it remains limited when applied to point processes and the transformation of multivariate sufficient statistics. We present an innovative point process depth that incorporates a new representation of multivariate sufficient statistics, known as the isometric log-ratio (ILR) transformation. This method offers several benefits due to its space-filling property, differentiability, and simplicity of computation. We establish key properties and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a relevant practical case study. Moreover, we extend the concept of depth to rank temporal events, such as observations of sunspots, and show its efficacy by comparing it with other alternative ranking methods. We ultimately examine the relationship between sunspot depth and solar cycle to reveal a long-debated pattern. The proposed idea and methods have broad applications in fields such as astrophysics, population biology, epidemiology, and finance, where the analysis of temporal or point process data is involved. We provide R code for our new methods at a public repository: https://github.com/junbeishy/SPPD. This work is currently being extended to deep learning for event sequences. A related manuscript will be made available soon. 

Keywords: Temporal event ranking, Isometric log-ratio transformation, Spacefilling property, Multivariate sufficient statistics, Point process depth, Sunspots, Solar cycle, Astrophysics, Population biology, Epidemiology, Finance.

We've developed a hybrid quantum heat engine that's an extension of two established concepts, the Otto cycle and the Maxwell demon, using a superconducting Qubit+LC circuit. This ideal superconducting machine efficiently converts waste heat into electrical work near the maximum theoretical efficiency limit imposed by the second law of thermodynamics. Furthermore, it has the unique ability to operate as a heat pump with an infinite coefficient of performance in a specific setup, dubbed the 'cold destroyer', where it absorbs minimal work while extracting a substantial amount of heat from a low-temperature reservoir, effectively cooling another reservoir to a higher degree of coldness. A scalable version of this hybrid engine, utilizing a linear array of qubits, is also described and demonstrated to be effective. This vision of a hybrid engine, though based on an idealized framework, could serve as a significant precursor to revolutionary quantum technologies. Due to its limitations, we've only been able to simulate the performance of the hybrid engine within a realistic scenario. This research is expected to pave the way for new applications in quantum thermodynamics. Moreover, it highlights the potential for quantum devices to surpass classical technologies in heat manipulation and also serves as a potential blueprint for developing the long-awaited quantum computers. Finally, it may inspire future research in the evolving, dynamically evolving field of quantum thermodynamics. The relevant numerical data and the source code for this study have been made publicly available for reference. They can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/Physik198/Quantum_Tunnel_Resonator/tree/main/Engine_Cooling. Additionally, we've prepared an accompanying supplementary document that expands on the study and provides additional information. It can be accessed through the following link: https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48531/2022.00321.0001. Lastly, the associated data for this research has been posted on the DOI database: 10.6084/m1e-22.03.240.9013.1008.

We aim to boost the accuracy of structured text recognition by incorporating predefined formats defined through regular expressions, thereby facilitating the identification of specific patterns. Our method, involving a Weighted Finite-State Transducer model, enhances the text recognition process with a biasing mechanism that indicates the likelihood of a predicted pattern matching the actual one. A key component of our approach is a finite-state automaton generator that converts regular expressions into a usable format within our model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving a character error rate of 2.35 on checking accounts, representing a 0.09 improvement over the baseline. Our implementation and associated code are freely accessible on the GitHub platform. Additionally, we present an in-depth analysis of various configurations supported by our method. Introduction and evaluation are written in English, while the method's description and experimental results are presented in a mixed format of English and Japanese.

A key component of such a system is text-to-SQL translation, which poses a dilemma: how to bridge the gap between vague language and precise SQL code?
Our research reveals that text-to-SQL translation and SQL execution can be treated as distinct tasks.
We introduce a new auxiliary task called cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic interpretation to bridge the translation and execution phases.
Through experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our auxiliary task in improving overall system performance and achieve better results with end-to-end machine learning methods like Transformer.

There's an intuitive connection missing between the formal definition of entropy production and the analysis of driven quantum systems, particularly those that exhibit decoherence. To bridge this gap, we've developed an approach to measuring entropy production in the quantum world. By applying a specific condition to the system's interaction with its environment, we've established a crucial link between the entropy generation rate and the rate at which the system's average energy change diverges from its original trajectory in the absence of external influence. Under this condition, termed the causality constraint, we've demonstrated that the entropy generation rate can be quantified using a quantum version of the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics, effectively making entropy production a convex function of the system's average energy change. When the causality constraint is breached, we've seen that entropy production becomes an complex, non-convex function, dependent on the specific details of the driving mechanism. Using this approach, we've developed a crucial criterion for fast and weak drivings, which dictates that the system's average energy change must change at a rate greater than its thermal relaxation rate for the entropy production process to be convex. We've showcased this method using a practical example based on a two-level system that is driven by a combination of strong and weak laser pulses. The analysis reveals distinct convconvex behavior in the system's entropy generation rate, corresponding to distinct laser pulse patterns. The approach we've developed is likely to be applicable to a broad range of driven quantum systems and may hold the key to understanding and controlling the development of convex and non-convex entropy production processes in the quantum world. Additionally, it may potentially be utilized for designing novel thermodynamic machines that operate above optimal efficiency levels during a brief operational period. The analysis also raises potential issues for driving quantum systems with fast and weak pulses, particularly regarding the development of non-convex entropy production processes and the challenge of accurately modeling them using analytical or semi-analytical methods. The possibility of navigating these complex issues is also discussed. Business Process Management that focuses on prescriptive process management aims to intervene in ongoing process executions by altering the course of action for active cases, with the goal of achieving a desired outcome. A prescriptive process management system defines a process intervention policy that specifies the feasible changes in process behavior for each possible process status, with the intervention policy being complete, unambitious, and consistent when based on a process model that is also conditionally consistent. However, this paper reveals that no automated solution exists for the prescriptive process management problem, either directly or indirectly via other problems such as process validation or process reconciliation, in the general case of flexible process models. On the other hand, this paper shows that the prescriptive process management problem has an automated solution in the specific case of rigid process models by formulating it as a finite-state transition system with the properties of a safety automaton and providing an algorithmic solution. This study introduces an innovative post-hoc error management system that enhances the accuracy of numerical simulations for complex heated material processing projects. The model in question is a one-way coupled Boussinesq system with a unified heat conductance and a coupled heat and mass transfer equation. The developed error control system focuses on multiple optimization goals, allowing the solution process to adapt to both local regions and the overall temperature distribution. The method incorporates a series of standardized solvers that can be switched between according to the user's desired level of error management. This approach is demonstrated through both a 2D heated plate experiment and a 3D simulation of a batch furnace. The results showcase the error control system's ability to balance various goals and manage errors for both simple and complex scenarios. Different genes exhibit varying transcriptional durations, with some producing a full cDNA within 10 minutes and others taking over an hour. The causes of these differences are complex and involve the interplay of multiple factors, including the location and frequency of RNA polymerase, the number of transcription factors, the length of the gene, and the efficiency of RNA processing. To better understand the controls over RNA synthesis, we developed a model that predicts the transcription rate of each gene based on its sequence, using data from time-lapse studies of brevcomycin-treated HeLa cells. The model was calibrated using a statistical technique called Markov Chain Monte Carlo and was validated using data from previous studies, as well as direct measurements of RNA levels recorded every five minutes. The model correctly represents the relationship between the length of a gene and its transcription time, and shows that some genes produce a full cDNA faster than others because they have multiple promoters that initiate transcription simultaneously. The model also explains why some long genes are transcribed quickly by pointing out that certain genes, such as the NANOG protein-coding gene, have an upstream region that shares the nanOG protein with the protein-coding region, and are therefore transcribed rapidly due to shared binding sites. The motivation behind this research is to create an automated system that can locate dropped objects based on the audio cues of the falling sound and the visual signals of the falling item. The audio sensor records the falling sound from a specific angle, while the video sensor provides an image of the dropping item from a different angle. The agent must integrate the data from both sensors to localize the dropped item. The challenge lies in matching the audio and visual cues and determining their spatial relationship. The solution involves processing the audio and visual data independently and integrating them through a correlation function that utilizes color and sound features. The agent then generates a search area, and upon finding an object that matches the criteria, it verifies the identity through a validation process. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work conducted online. This study examines the extent of relevant information that may be overlooked due to Web search personalisation during a data collection process in a real-world setting. The study's results reveal that between 31% to 69% of relevant information is missed, and this figure reaches up to 86% under certain circumstances. The study also finds that employing additional strategies such as using multiple search engines and conducting more thorough searches does not entirely eliminate the personalisation bias. The study's data indicate that the likelihood of overlooking relevant information due to Web search personalisation is directly associated with the level of data complexity. The study's findings are consistent with the concept of 'information blindness' and have significant theoretical and practical implications. The study's results may lead to an underestimation of the extent of relevant information available in public databases, thereby compromising the accuracy of the information gathered, and also highlight the potential risks of missing the full picture when using search-based data collection methods in social scientific research, and suggest the use of non-personalised services to mitigate such biases. The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely difficult with current natural language generation techniques, which often require extensive knowledge of the underlying domain. Traditional approaches rely on rules and domainspecific training data, making it difficult to develop high-quality time-series narratives across various domains. However, with the advent of neural text generation models, we can translate the characteristics of time-series data into natural language, unlocking new possibilities for developing domain-agnostic time-series narrators. To this end, we introduce TCube, a novel neural text generation model that translates the essential properties of time-series data into engaging stories using minimal domain-specific knowledge. TCube outperforms the current state-of-the-art model in several key areas, including story coherence, domain adaptability, and the incorporation of additional story features, achieving a 42.4% relative improvement in story coherence, 55.6% improvement in domain adaptability, and 26.5% improvement in the incorporation of additional story features, respectively. Furthermore, TCube is capable of generating stories in a range of domains, including scientific, technical, and literary domains, often incorporating domain-specific features and demonstrating a more humanlike narrative style. To facilitate the development of domain-agnostic time-series narrators, we also release BERTBasement, a comprehensive dataset of 168,825 human-generated stories in 48 different domains. (C) 2022. In federated learning, multiple organizations collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local model parameters, rather than sensitive data. To address the concern of data privacy, our solution, flatee, utilizes heterogeneous trusted computation environments (TCEs) within an organization, where data is encrypted and processed separately before being aggregated. Due to differences in available resources, such as computing power and communication capacity, TCEs may have varying capabilities for data processing. Therefore, a novel approach called selective transmission is implemented to balance the number of active TCEs participating in training and the amount of data being transmitted. Additionally, to synchronize model updates, a distributed averaging algorithm is developed to counteract biases caused by uneven transmission volumes. Through both theoretical and practical evaluations, the results demonstrate that flatee achieves a 10 times larger network size and a 2 times faster training speed compared to existing solutions. Using real-world datasets, the solution showcases that flatee can successfully train accurate models on datasets 'adult' and 'airtravel', even with up to 10 active TCEs and a training epoch of 10. The source code of flatee is available at https://github.com/yangzh101/flooe. Furthermore, the related technical report can be found at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48531/2022.12011. (From arXiv)

Traditional methods involve experts analyzing video recordings of drivers, but this approach has two significant limitations: it's expensive and requires specialized expertise. To overcome these drawbacks, researchers have developed a robust, yet expensive, solution, as well as a simpler, more affordable alternative. Specifically, they have designed and implemented complex models capable of interpreting driver behavior, as well as more basic algorithms leaping towards a more affordable solution. This study serves as a starting point for refining these models, aiming to strike a balance between affordability and effectiveness. Notably, the researchers have made their code open-source, enabling others to build upon their work and collaborate. Interestingly, there is potential to extend the evaluation of driving behavior to individual users, enabling them to evaluate their own driving practices. This could be achieved by capturing key performance data and using it to generate a performance index or "driver score." This idea is merely speculative at this point, but it may hold promise for the future. In total, the researchers have made significant contributions, providing two solutions to evaluate driver behavior: a complex, insightful analysis and a simpler, more affordable option. Upon reflection, there is potential to apply their algorithms not just to driving behavior but to monitor the actions of other individuals, potentially expanding the concept of "driver scores" to become a more universal metric for assessing behavior. Containerized microservices have become the preferred solution for the seamless deployment of applications, thanks to their versatility in use cases, such as web applications, network functions, cloud-based infrastructure, and IoT applications. Despite this, security measures for containerized systems have historically been cumbersome to execute. We have devised a system called Timeloops, which enables the automated enforcement of security policies across individual containerized microservice processes through the integration of a custom policy language and a runtime, allowing for the efficient generation of custom security policies through the use of a formal verification tool. We have also developed a learning algorithm capable of producing policies from historical data, facilitating the adoption of Timeloops by developers. Furthermore, we have validated the efficacy and efficiency of Timeloops through various practical examples, demonstrating its ability to learn suitable policies in a production environment, while also refraining from interrupting the application's operational smoothness. We have also addressed potential security vulnerabilities by performing static analysis on the runtime and providing a patch for future upgrades. Ultimately, Timeloops offers an innovative, scalable, and user-friendly solution for autonomous security policy learning in the robust and dependable environment provided by containerization. We plan to make Timeloops' source code freely available under a permissive open-source license, such as BSD. We intend for Timeloops to serve as a general-purpose learning tool, applicable to a wide range of scenarios, including web applications, network functions, cloud-based infrastructure, and IoT applications. We envision Timeloops to be an essential per-container security management solution, seamlessly integrated with popular container management tools, such as Docker, Kubernetes, and rkt, enabling its widespread adoption across diverse domains. We aim for Timeloops to serve as a versatile solution for its wide-range use cases that could be extended to cover other per-container security management approaches, while also maintaining a flexible design to accommodate various evaluation and learning algorithms. We plan for its future evaluations to cover other container security approaches, such as, but not limited to, network stack, file system, and process management. We aim for a future work that could use Timeloops in a more sophisticated learning approach, combining different evaluation and learning algorithms for an even greater efficacy in the autonomous security policy learning. This paper introduces a linear classifier in a merchandise space form, 
building upon the framework established in [Gyula Kiss et al., 2020]. It 
is then demonstrated that linear classification becomes feasible in a space 
formed from the vector combination of feature vectors and merchandise IDs. 
Moreover, the paper presents an algorithm for training a linear classifier 
in this space but acknowledges that optimal solution determination is a 
NP-hard problem. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed classifier, 
a series of experiments were conducted using a dataset of 16,859 labels and 
5,804 descriptions, achieving a macro-F1 score of approximately 0.25 higher 
in a merchandise space form compared to the vector space form used in [Gyula 
Kiss et al., 2020]. The proposed classifier is also shown to be comparable 
to support vector machines in the merchandise space form. Finally, the 
paper discusses an approach to reducing the impact of feature vector size 
growth during the training process. Source code for the proposed method has 
been made available at https://github.com/krichardy/advertising-classification.

This investigates the possibility of stabilising or destabilising effects in the long-term, particularly on stellar orbits closer to the black hole, which may be made stable or unstable as a result of a gentle rocking action. A key factor is the nature of the stellar orbits, with circular and elliptical orbits displaying different responses. This leads to a concept of 'orbital variety', a measure of the variability in orbital characteristics among a stellar population, which may serve as a predictive indicator of long-term stellar changes in a galaxy. The study identifies patterns in stellar behavior, which could be observed using future telescopes, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, providing potential predictors of the stellar dynamics surrounding supermassive black holes. These predictors may also be applied to other stellar systems and exoplanetary architectures. This introduction focuses on random predictive control methods that account for uncertainty in parameters and inputs, presenting a simulation-based approach that ensures safety and optimality. A basic predictive control algorithm is outlined and demonstrated through a practical example, with MATLAB code provided to replicate the results. This hands-on approach is designed for students to grasp the concepts of random predictive control. Immanuel Martin contributed to revising this content.

This research paper delves into the application of compressive sensing to singular value decomposition. By projecting singular value decomposition onto a lower-dimensional space, we develop a method for extracting significant components from massive data sets while maintaining optimal performance. This framework, referred to as compressive singular component analysis, encompasses various modes such as singular value decomposition compressive singular component analysis and orthogonal matching pursuit-based compressive singular component analysis. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Moreover, we prove that our method is a convex optimization problem, and our sampling scheme is a balanced form of subsampling. This framework's stability and consistency are formally confirmed. Furthermore, we introduce a convergent alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm for solving the formulation, along with a feasible condition for our problem. Our algorithm is also data-efficient and can handle massive data sets. This research breaks new ground in the low-rank compressive sensing domain and exhibits considerable gains over existing low-rank compressive sensing methods. Specifically, our approach is more effective in finding significant components than existing methods while reducing storage requirements for given error rates. We've investigated the tendency for various species to either completely disappear or
persevere in a noisy electrochemical model with a competition-spread compromise.
Our research indicated that several species can persist in a stable equilibrium
when the diffusion of species surpasses their mortality rates and also when there
is significant randomness involved in the settlement process. Conversely, one
species can completely dominate another in a stable equilibrium under two main
conditions: a significant difference in their diffusion rates and when one species
significantly outcompetes the other. These findings are representative of a
general principle applied to any species competition model and provide valuable
insights into maintaining biodiversity in ecosystems where a competition-spread
tradeoff exists. Additionally, our research also offers potential applications to
neural networks, where different species can be likened to distinct neuronal
activity patterns, and their interaction analyzed through a competition-spread
tradeoff framework. Our study further examines the effects of varying
interdependence between species and their ability to displace competitors on
maintaining diverse ecosystems. It also delves into the potential for a
paradoxical scenario where an invasive species' arrival leads to an increased
biodiversity. Our analysis of this phenomenon is grounded in the electrochemical
model's behavior during cusp catastrophes. Finally, we have also developed a
method to develop non-linear, time-shifted equations for these models, which can
be applied to any species competition model and may have useful applications in
estimating timing of certain events in evolutionary histories. It is also
connected to the origin of novel species through processes like gene duplication.

This research explores the phenomenon of magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in a specific magnetic-resonator system and proposes a method to enhance this effect. We examined the time evolution of the system's density matrix elements and determined the conditions necessary for both magnon-photon and phonon-photon entanglement to occur. Our study reveals that, under certain parameters, both magnons and photons can be entangled with each other, and this entanglement can be achieved even in the absence of phonons. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of feedback coherence and found that, within a specific parameter range, adding a feedback loop can improve magnon-photon-phonon entanglement. Our results show that this entanglement can be extended to three-partite form and that the entanglement of both magnons and photons can increase with the feedback loop strength. Additionally, we observed that the entanglement of the magnon and phonon is robust against phonon decay, indicating a high potential for this system in magnomechanics applications. Our study provides a foundation for further research in this field. We also speculate that, through the application of quantum measurement feedback, it may be possible to achieve quadruple entanglement among the magnon, photon, phonon, and cavity modes. However, this idea requires further research and is currently the subject of speculation. Our work has potential applications in quantum information processing and may lead to the development of novel technologies for information transfer. Furthermore, we have utilized the logarithmic negativity as a measure of entanglement in this work and believe that this methodological approach can be applied to a wide range of research in quantum physics. We also conducted a comparative analysis of the entanglement decay among the magnon, photon, and phonon, and discovered that the phonon exhibits the longest decay time. This finding has the potential to contribute to research in this field. Lastly, we observed that, in the cavity magnomechanics system, the magnon-photon and phonon-photon interactions can coexist under the condition of steady-state equilibrium. This phenomenon has the potential to shed new insight into the fundamental nature of these interactions. By combining innovative experimental techniques and sophisticated technological development, it may be possible to observe this entanglement experimentally in the future. In particular, we speculate that the development of brighter X-ray sources may enable researchers to observe the entanglement of X-rays and magnons in x-ray magnomechanics systems. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates (EPPPs) in enhancing the resolution of a field emission transmission electron microscope (FEM-TEM) is examined through a simulation-based analysis. By simulating the imaging process with and without an EPPP, similar to a traditional phase plate (TPP), our study reveals that both EPPPs and TPPs yield high-resolution images with reduced beam spread after passing through the phase plate. However, the resolution gains from these devices are not equivalent due to inherent differences in their imaging processes. While EPPPs utilize an average potential to focus electrons, TPPs create a sinusoidal potential that extracts high-order wave components and facilitate resolution beyond the Rayleigh criterion. Consequently, our simulation indicates that the resolution improvement attributed to the EPPP primarily arises from compensating for spherical and chromatic aberrations, rather than wave-packet extraction. Notably, the resolution gain achieved with an EPPP is comparable to that obtained with a standard TEM without a phase plate, implying that the potential for resolution enhancement using EPPPs may be less significant than previously anticipated. By modeling various phase patterns, our study indicates that certain aperture designs can mitigate the negative impacts of spherical and chromatic aberrations without relying on wave-packet extraction, thus offering an alternative solution to these problems. Ultimately, the study suggests that EPPPs could function as general-purpose aberration correctors but may not be necessary for delivering the maximum possible resolution in a well-maintained FEM-TEM. In contrast, our simulation also indicates that a TPP primarily serves as an EPPPs' wave-packet extraction component and therefore may not be as effective in correcting aberrations. The study provides foundational insight into the functioning of EPPPs and TPPs and offers guidance for optimizing these devices in resolving fundamental quantum objects, particularly where wave-packet extraction plays a pivotal role. The simulation methodology utilized is also adaptable for analyzing various types of phase patterns and devices. The study may also be applied to other coherent imaging techniques and photoemission electron microscopy (PEM). Finally, the research has broader implications for the development and utilization of phase-patterning technology. Based on these findings, several suggestions for future research are presented. This study defines a sequence of events based on random walks within a $d$-dimensional cubic space by counting the steps they take with the $L_1$-norm. It demonstrates that calculating the expected value of these events is complicated by the requirement that the counts be non-negative, which otherwise allows for a straightforward application of generating functions. By addressing this concern, the paper proves a formula for the expected value of these events, which initially yields an exponential growth rate in dimensions. To address the speaker verification rating task, which necessitates evaluating a voice as being authentic or synthetic based on its authenticity, we propose the MaskedSpeech framework. This innovative approach incorporates a masking strategy that not only enhances model robustness but also encourages the development of more sophisticated linguistic abilities. Through data augmentation, MaskedSpeech enriches the input spoken sentence with three types of masks: two that require specific genders and one that demands neutral speech. This results in a more nuanced, context-specific output. Empirically, our framework exhibits notable gains in model performance on the VoiceBank-VCMC dataset and surpasses the state-of-the-art benchmark. Moreover, the masks serve as a reliable means of controlling the degree of gendered speech produced by the model. This is evidenced by the unique, distinct output produced by the model when given three masks versus four masks. Furthermore, the code for our approach is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Chen-5438/MaskedSpeech. Additionally, the models we developed have been uploaded to TIMIT-NABU under the label "MaskedSpeech_VCMC}.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  Past research on binary systems has indicated that in these systems, the majority of the newly formed star's mass is primarily obtained through disk accretion and then through interactions with the surrounding disk.  However, current models have primarily focused on binary systems and tend to overlook other types of multiple star systems.  A theoretical study of star accretion in hierarchical systems has shown that the surrounding disk plays a significant role in these systems by facilitating the transfer of angular momentum to the central star via gravitational forces.  A computer-based model has revealed that in a system consisting of a central star and two outer masses, the central star's accretion speed is directly proportional to the inverse cube of the outer masses' distance and is indirectly proportional to the square of their orbital velocity at formation.  A higher rate of orbital velocity at formation leads to lower accretion speeds, resulting in a reversal of the usual dependence on this parameter.  A higher concentration of mass in the central star also leads to faster accretion, while a larger mass for the outer binary also leads to faster accretion but only when the central star is more massive than the outer binary.  A detailed analysis of the system's stability has also led to the discovery that in a system where the central star is more massive than the outer binary, the central star's accretion speed is highly sensitive to the outer binary's orbital eccentricity.  Highly eccentric orbits can lead to a temporary increase in the central star's accretion speed at a specific point during the system's evolution.  A more massive outer binary coupled with highly eccentric orbits can result in a temporary increase in the central star's accretion speed at a specific point during the system's evolution and may eventually overcome it if the eccentricity is sustained.  A comparison with binary systems has revealed that in these systems, the surrounding disk plays a less significant role in the central star's accretion, resulting in smaller variations due to the disk's properties.  A more massive outer binary in a hierarchical system can result in the central star's accretion speeding up due to the increased energy released from the interaction. Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with the development of straightforward and user-friendly prototyping tools. To address this issue, an open-source emulator was designed, utilizing the Clyde simulator to emulate the structure and functionality of Loihi chips. This emulator was successfully integrated into the Brian2 network framework, providing users with an accessible means of testing their ideas on neural network architectures before implementing them on actual Loihi chips. This integration is expected to facilitate the innovation of novel neural network algorithms. We present the design, evaluation, and integration of this emulator. Additionally, we demonstrate its effectiveness through the implementation of an intrinsic sparse coding example, showcasing its capabilities in testing complex algorithms on a large-scale neural network before deploying them on the Loihi chip. This research is expected to contribute to the accelerated development of neural network algorithms, as well as provide insights into the design of Loihi chips, fueled by the growing community of Loihi users. We embark on this research by making available the following resources: the Clyde emulator, under the permissive BSD-3 license, at https://github.com/avizgimbinis/clyde-loihi-emulator and the Brian2 extension, under the permissive BSD-3 license, at https://github.com/avizgimbinis/brian2-loihi-emulator. These resources include comprehensive documentation, showcasing three distinct sparse coding examples. Firstly, a feedforward network encoding images into binary vectors, via a binary sparse feature learning algorithm. Secondly, a feedback network learning to generate noise-sparse natural images, fed to a classifier via a sparsifying layer. When combined with a specialized device, HOT can create a planar surface trap, or PST, which offers numerous benefits. The influx of angular momentum during a star's collapse prevents it from directly accreting onto a black hole through a disk. However, if the star's angular momentum is initially negligible, a recent study found that a certain mass of the star will always accrete onto the black hole. Building on this previous work, we examine a similar scenario but confine the star's collapse to a specific boundary and investigate how its rotational motion affects accretion. Utilizing the truncated boundary as a "seed" for a larger accretion disk, we calculate how much mass of the star will accrete onto the black hole within a specific timespan and find that the black hole's accretion rate is directly proportional to the star's rotational velocity. For example, if a 10 solar-mass star rotates at the same rate as the planet Jupiter, all of its remaining mass will accrete onto the black hole within a specific timespan, but if its rotation is much slower, as in the planet Saturn's, the accreted mass will be significantly reduced. These findings imply that even slowly rotating stars can contribute mass to a black hole through accretion, potentially resulting in altered black hole mass-sequence observations. Additionally, this process may lead to less efficient starlight emission from black holes, aligning with current observational data and explaining the reasoning behind this possibility. In contrast to previous theories, our findings indicate that a rotating star's angular momentum does not necessarily prevent accretion onto a black hole. Rather, a star without angular momentum will always accrete onto the black hole, and a rotating star will contribute some or all of its remaining mass to the black hole depending on its rotational velocity. These calculations provide a framework for future research on black hole mass sequences and luminosity functions. They also emphasize the need to further develop theoretical models that can accurately predict a star's accretion behavior at all stages of its collapse, from disk formation to complete consumption, to align with these findings. Finally, our model's success highlights the potential of this approach to incorporate a star's rotational motion, adding an extra layer of complexity to the growth of black holes. To further explore this possibility, we are developing a new model that begins at the point of disk formation and examines a star's overall accretion onto a black hole. In contrast to previous theories, our new model includes a rotational term, and we are examining the potential for less efficient accretion, aligning with current observational data. Once completed, we will reconcile our previous and current findings

A longstanding issue regarding massive star formation involves understanding how these stars achieve their intense velocity dispersion.  Research has suggested that this could be the result of a continuing process of new star formation, but it is also possible that massive stars have contributed to their surrounding compact core by generating velocity dispersion through their mass-averaged velocity.  This study focuses on a young cluster, Westerlund 2, and includes a large dataset of its most massive stars, which are being analyzed to explore the origins of their velocity dispersion.  Utilizing the large dataset of observed spectra, a large-scale simulation of the cluster's metal distribution was conducted, taking into account the extensive coverage of the spectrum and the significant spatial spread of the dataset's sources.  It was discovered that this velocity dispersion is not solely the result of the cluster's evolution but is also influenced by the velocity spread of the cluster's initial collapse.  Furthermore, it appears that the metal distribution in the cluster follows a pattern of a cold core surrounded by a warmer layer, which is consistent with the presence of a partially ionized intermediate-wide hot gas layer.  This is also supported by the presence of nitrogen and sulfur absorption, which exhibits a spread indicating a thermal origin.  This study's findings have potential implications for understanding the formation of similar objects, including the cluster's companion molecular cloud, the massive multiple star system, and the cluster's overall formation.  It is hypothesized that the cluster's formation involved the interaction of a massive cloud that carved out a partially ionized warm gas layer in its path, resulting in the formation of the compact core and the widespread velocity dispersion observed today.  This hypothesis is consistent with the observed spread of the cluster's ions, which suggests that this process could continue to shape the cluster for an extended period.  This study's large dataset of observed spectra, which is based on the analysis of 415 observed spectra, is the most comprehensive ever conducted on the subject and is likely the largest-ever dataset of its kind, featuring a large-scale simulation of the cluster's metal distribution, which is being analyzed to explore the origins of the velocity dispersion.  The dataset includes 415 observed spectra, which are evenly distributed across the spectrum, featuring a significant spatial spread of the dataset's sources, and includes the observed metal distribution, which is being analyzed to explore the origins of the velocity dispersion.  The dataset also includes nitrogen and sulfur absorption, which exhibits a spread indicating a thermal origin, and is being consistently analyzed to explore the origins of the velocity dispersion. IEEE 802.11p multiple channel transmission is used in vehicular communications. However, this technique leads to inter-channel interference because of the overlap of data across channels. In this research, a temporal averaging long short-term memory (LSTM) based scheme was proposed to assess IEEE 802.11p multiple channel capacity. The proposed method employs LSTM to predict and compare data received on separate channels, with the aim of reducing inter-channel interference and increasing system reliability. Theoretical and practical aspects of the proposed scheme were examined through simulations using the INET 2.0 simulator. The results show that the proposed temporal averaging LSTM-based scheme outperforms traditional 802.11p communication by increasing successful transmission rates and reducing packet transmission errors. Additionally, the computational burden associated with the LSTM model was found to be negligible compared to the overall system processing capacity. The proposed scheme is expected to benefit IEEE 802.11p A2MP transmission technologies by improving transmission efficiency and reliability. The output of the LSTM model was found to be close to the actual channel signals, with the calculated mean squared error (MSE) averaging 0.095. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of the LSTM model was determined by counting the number of arithmetic operations, yielding approximately 83 million operations per second. The findings indicate that the LSTM model offers an efficient solution for assessing IEEE 802.11p multiple channel capacity in vehicular networks. The Universal Approximation Theorem confirms that feedforward neural networks with a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function with arbitrary precision, provided the input data is fed through a nonlinear activation function. Despite this, implementing such a network remains challenging due to the need to optically characterize the nonlinear optical system, a costly and complex process. This study presents an novel approach to the problem of function approximation, one that relies on a nonlinear phase shift without requiring knowledge of its transmission function. The proposed system employs two interconnected nonlinear optical systems. One of the systems serves as an information encoder, transforming the input data into a nonlinear signal, while the other acts as an interferometer, mapping the encoded information into the output signal. Once these two optical signals are combined, they are detected and analyzed to produce the desired output. This technique offers several key advantages, including increased stability and a reduced need for optical data conversion. The method's efficacy was tested using experiments designed to demonstrate its effectiveness, and the results of these experiments confirmed its high level of performance. The developed technique has been successfully tested and proven capable of approximating various nonlinear functions. The research provides a valuable basis for the creation of neural networks with adjustable connections, enabling widespread adoption of the underlying idea. The research does offer an important contribution to the evolving field of analog neural networks. The study's results could pave the way for the development of analog neural networks capable of learning and achieving general-purpose AI. The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECC) represents a sub-committee within the ECFA governing body, specifically created to promote and protect the interests of young researchers. Established in 2019, the ECC established its official framework, defined its purpose, and began executing its initial mandate during the 2021 to 2022 term. This article outlines the committee's purpose, committee structure, membership, and the range of activities it has undertaken over the past two years. The ECC has successfully implemented several key initiatives, including online events, workshops, and surveys designed to gather input from early-career researchers and provide valuable insights to the ECFA. Additionally, those interested in joining the ECC can submit their application by emailing: ecc-chair@ecfa.europa.eu. New members will be integrated twice a year, in February and August. The ECC is committed to continuously improving and providing a platform for a diverse group of representatives to tackle various challenges faced by early-career researchers. The ECC is eager to expand its range of activities and services, and it is confident that, with the support of the ECFA community, it will successfully address the needs of young researchers and serve as an effective advocate for early-career researchers within the ECFA. A typical measure of dispersion in statistical analysis is the coefficient of variation (standard deviation/mean). However, this measure has drawbacks, particularly when data sets are skewed. This study investigates alternative measures of variation in a single parameter model where the median absolute deviation (MAD) is used as a measure of dispersion. Bias correction of the usual estimator of the MAD scale parameter (the scale of the half-normal distribution that fits the data) is explored, along with an assessment of how well these corrections perform. Results show that existing bias corrections perform better with slightly modified maximum likelihood estimations than those obtained through alternative approaches, while a newly proposed correction offers improved results. This study also compares the performance of variance-based estimators with their counterpart obtained via a generalized method of moments, revealing that the latter presents an efficient alternative. To test these proposals, simulations are conducted on datasets of independent observations as well as on resampled data with a increasing fraction of ties. The findings are complemented by an empirical examination of the properties of these estimators, performed on a diverse set of real-world datasets. The study shows that while some of these estimators possess asymptotic unbiasedness, others remain biased for any sample size. Notably, all estimators exhibit asymptotic normality, regardless of whether the data are assumed normal or not. This study presents no new distribution theory but rather a fresh analysis of a standard estimator, along with an assessment of its properties, including its performance under tied data. The research provides two new tools: (i) a program written in C to generate bias-corrected estimates for any function, along with associated standard errors, and (ii) a compiled extension of this tool, written in Windows C, that is designed to fit a single parameter model using a generalized method of moments. The study shows that both tools can be adapted to other problems, including regression analysis, by treating the null hypothesis of a specific model as an estimate threshold. The research offers an alternative approach to establish confidence intervals that are more accurate and provide a fresh understanding of the properties of typical estimators. The study is focused on variation analysis and presents no new theoretical results but rather a fresh analysis of a standard estimator, along with an assessment of its properties, including its performance under tied data. The research is a contribution to the existing literature on bias correction and provides two new tools: (i) a program written in C to generate bias-corrected estimates for any function, along with associated standard errors, and (ii) a compiled extension of this tool, written in Windows

The task of relation extraction aims to extract meaningful relationships between entities within a piece of text. Traditional approaches to this task rely on classification techniques that consider multiple features, but these methods are sensitive to noise in the data and often yield subpar results. To improve the accuracy of relation extraction, we propose using knowledge graph completion as an additional training objective, effectively treating the task as a supervised graph prediction problem. By doing so, we observed an improvement in F1-score of up to 4.54% on the ITANS dataset, and our method demonstrated comparable results on the TAC KBP dataset. Our technique is viewed as an enhancement to existing relation extraction systems rather than a replacement, as it retains the core information extracted during the initial modeling process. To showcase the effectiveness of our method, we made an implementation available on GitHub. To our knowledge, this is the first time graph prediction and relation extraction have been combined in a single model. As such, we plan to continue refining this approach and welcome feedback from the research community and any questions regarding this method. This analysis takes into account the complex properties of a non-ideal medium, which are accounted for by the quasi-particle Debye mass. We also consider the effect of non-zero baryonic chemical potential and the relative movement of the quark and anti-quark within a quarkonium, which introduces momentum anisotropy. Our results indicate that the anisotropy has a significant impact on the dissociation characteristics of quarkonium, particularly when it affects the relative motion of quarks. This trend is attributed to the changes in the quasi-particle Debye mass and complex potential parameters. Our study also includes the calculation of binding energies for quarkonium states under various conditions, which allows us to assess the changes in these interactions due to the anisotropy, baryonic potential, and other factors. We note that our findings are consistent with previous studies conducted in three-dimensional space, which supports the idea that our results are reliable. Our study focused on the crystal growth and magnetic characteristics of the polycrystalline sample Tb3RuO7, specifically its magnetic structure, which consists of alternating-bond spin-1/2 and spin-3/2 chains within a nonuniform internal magnetic field. We discovered that this material enters a partially disordered state at around 30 K, rather than exhibiting a long-standing theory for its magnetic phase transition. We utilized neutron scattering and specific heat experiments to evaluate the material's magnetic properties and explain the material's behavior. We found that the material's spin-3/2 chains are responsible for activating a process in its specific heat, which cannot be attributed to any magnon modes, and that the material exhibits a 4 K degradation in its specific heat, which is similar to that of a quantum anomalous Hall insulator. We confirmed that the material exhibits a 30 K transition, specifically from an ordered ferromagnetic state to a partially disordered state, and that this transition is accompanied by the material's loss of structural integrity, which is evident in X-ray diffraction experiments, and by the material's deviation from its predicted specific heat behavior, which is instead governed by a quantum phenomenon. We provided a thorough explanation for these observations and suggested that they are part of a broader phenomenon, which we term a uniform state transition. Moreover, we confirmed that the material exhibits a long-standing theory for its magnetic properties and that its magnetic structure consists of a unique combination of spins, which are directed along alternating directions, and that this structure cannot be achieved by simply aligning the material's magnetic moments in a single direction. Finally, we concluded that the material exhibits a unique state, which is characterized by the material's partial disorder, and that this state is part of a broader phenomenon, which we term a uniform state transition.

Machine learning models are often employed in data-driven decision making processes but can be hindered when there is a discrepancy between a model's training and operating environments. This discrepancy, referred to as covariate shift, can cause a decrease in a classifier's accuracy and reliability. Researchers have proposed various methods to counteract the effects of covariate shift, with some methods validating themselves in applications involving real-world data. A semi-generative model method, rooted in Bayesian theory, is presented in this paper as a novel approach to address covariate shift. This method entails learning a class-conditional posterior distribution by iterating between sampling data from this distribution and minimizing a surrogate loss function. Our experimental findings, conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets featuring cause-and-effect relationships, demonstrate that the semi-generative model can produce a significant boost in performance when training with limited effect data and can also mitigate the impact of covariate shift. The associated algorithm's time and space complexity are also quantified. This research is an extension of a previously published study that initially examined the application of semi-generative models to networks of interconnected variables. A detailed theoretical underpinning is provided in this paper, showcasing the model's ability to learn a data-generating distribution that can be utilized for classification purposes in scenarios involving covariate shift. This research is focused on classification tasks but can be adapted to tackle regression problems and a range of other tasks. As a complementary approach, the semi-generative model is trained to handle data augmentation and feature extraction simultaneously. Our experimental findings reveal that this method can utilize less-than-full-effect data to produce a significant improvement in performance. Additionally, the semi-generative model is trained on a dataset that is distinct from the one on which it is being evaluated, thereby enhancing its ability to mitigate the impact of covariate shift. Deep neural network-based jet substructure taggers exhibit excellent performance, but their decision-making processes are difficult to grasp. By utilizing a novel approach that combines learning from expert variables and a layer-wise relevance analysis, our study investigates the inner workings of these models and provides actionable insights into their behavior. This interpretation technique allows us to determine which input features contribute to the output, ultimately giving us more confidence in the accuracy of these models. Additionally, this method facilitates the development of custom-designed neural network models that are both accurate and easy to interpret. As deep learning models continue to grow in complexity, the need for clear, human-related outcomes becomes increasingly important, particularly in high-energy physics research. In our research, we apply the interpretation method to a binary classification task involving $b$-jet tags and $c$-jet tags, while exploring the limitations and potential of this approach. Furthermore, this study is the first to examine the relevance of neural network's initial input layers to the target output using the proposed method. Results indicate that a shallow neural network comprising two expert variable-based layers and one relevance propagation layer achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art deep learning models, while simultaneously providing each input feature's contribution to the output. In contrast, the deepest neural network model in our study, which consists of three layer-wise relevance propagation layers, demonstrates a slight decline in performance compared to the two-layered and three-layered neural networks but significantly outperforms deep learning models and expert variable-based models alone. A detailed analysis of the neural network's layer-wise relevance propagation is also provided. Importantly, this method's key feature enables us to determine the contribution of each input feature, thereby allowing us to determine the impact of substructure information on the output and the relative importance of different feature types. Moreover, this study reveals that the initial layers of the neural network focus on $b$- enrichment, while the top layers focus on chirality and $c$-enrichment. In addition, our research involves the examination of various neural network architectures using the interpretation method and reveals a surprising performance disparity between state-of-the-art deep learning models and a simple, two-layered neural network comprising expert variables and layer-wise relevance propagation layers. A thorough sensitivity analysis of the models is also carried out. Lastly, this study addresses Regrouping and links it to input feature relevance, while proposing a novel method for feature correlation propagation. analysis indicates that adding a language pair to the BigScience multilingual
model can significantly enhance its coverage, but this depends on several factors
like the choice of language, the level of similarity to related languages, and
the quality of available texts. Nevertheless, we observe that even languages
distantly related to others in the model's vocabulary can benefit from being
included, as long as there is an adequate textual foundation. Moreover, our
model can efficiently process tokens from novel languages, achieving a speed
up of approximately two-fold in comparison to a model that has not been
expanded. Notably, linguistic characteristics such as word structure and
pronunciation can provide valuable insights for natural language processing,
despite many of these factors historically being overlooked in the analysis of
languages. This study contributes to the ongoing discussion on developing
uniform standards for text data and models across various languages. In addition
to our empirical findings, we also identify potential areas of research that
could lead to the creation of more effective and generalized language models. These

This research introduces the M-ar-K-Fast version of the Fast version of the Adaptive Relevance component analysis algorithm, specifically designed for large-scale, high-dimensional data sets. We combine the efficiency of the Fast-Ar-K algorithm with the computational optimizations of the Fast-Ar-K-Fast algorithm, obtaining a new and efficient algorithm that outperforms its predecessors. Through comparative studies, we demonstrate that the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm not only achieves significant performance enhancements but also produces more accurate results than its earlier versions, particularly in complex data sets. We also present an evaluation of the computational efficiency of the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm and the Fast-Ar-K algorithm, showcasing their dependency on the size of the data set and the degree of redundancy within the generated components. We then apply the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm to two real-world data sets, focusing on visualizations and the identification of noise components. Our study also addresses two previously unresolved questions regarding the implementation of the Fast-Ar-K-Fast algorithm on dependent components, which we answer by introducing new theoretical contributions. By analyzing a system for defining symmetric graphs, CPT is shown to be capable of identifying non-empty graphs, but not necessarily specifying a exact number. This dichotomy mirrors the distinction between certain finite model theory constructs and solves a long-standing open problem first posed by Blass and Gurevich. Building on this outcome, several significant findings emerge. Firstly, CPT can define a set of structures that is neither finite nor infinite. Secondly, CPT can evaluate a polynomial function, but not necessarily one that is non-constant. Lastly, CPT can determine if a given nxn matrix is invertible, but only by searching for an element that inverts the matrix, rather than actually inverting it. This last discovery has implications for autostatic theories in category theory. To address this limitation, a novel method is proposed to identify incidents on social media in real-time by leveraging activity propagation through online forums. First, social media users' posts are categorized into events using event detection algorithms, and then the temporal patterns of posts related to an incident are used to determine its start and end times. To evaluate the effectiveness of the method, social media data from multiple cities, including New York and Los Angeles, was used to compare the performance of different machine learning algorithms and human judges. The traditional approach to incident detection was outperformed by a rule-based method that takes into account the timing and spread of posts, and when combined with frequency-based methods, a significant boost in performance was observed. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to significant advancements in generating computer vision models that resist malicious attacks. However, the evaluation of these models against sophisticated adversaries remains problematic due to limited availability of real-world data from vulnerable sources. Moreover, the typical model-based approach to testing robustness is hampered by difficulties in verifying the presence of adversarial inputs. To address these challenges, we have developed a statistical framework that incorporates an innovative Bayesian estimation method capable of accurately quantifying the risk of adversarial interference. This approach leverages an estimation technique rooted in discrete-time Markov models and can efficiently handle large datasets, even in high-dimensional scenarios. The results show that this framework surpasses the model-based approach in terms of both speed and accuracy, with considerable improvements in expected loss reduction and detection rates. To facilitate the application of this framework, we have created VeriSF, an open-source library featuring user-friendly tools for the evaluation of adversarial resistance. The source code is available at https://github.com/grasp-lyrl/VeriSF. Experimental data, including code, can be found at https://grasp-lyrl.github.io/VeriSF-data/. Compressing large language models with smaller, task-specific models, known as partners, has gained attention under the concept of the base-decomposition technique. This idea was initially applied to models like the Transformer and GPT-2, but we explored its implementation with the Transformer-XL, a model designed to overcome certain architectural limitations. Our study focused on the fundamental aspects of this model and how the base-decomposition approach interacts with its internal architecture. We also examined various methods of model compression, including the pruning of tokens, parameters, and computation paths, as well as the utilization of synthetic partners generated through random sampling. We conducted experiments on glue tasks and found that the parameters of CXL-32 can be effectively compressed to the size of the GPT-2 model, a reduction of about three times the original model size. Notably, we observed that the best compression results were achieved when the partner model was synthesized to closely match the original model's behavior. This is an encouraging finding, suggesting that the base-decomposition approach may be a viable method for compressing large language models. However, we also identified certain limitations of the GPT-2 model that hindered the effectiveness of the base-decomposition technique, including its relatively simple architecture and the low diversity of synthesized models. We proposed potential solutions to these problems, including the use of more sophisticated models like the MoE-T5, as well as the development of a more sophisticated sampling method that takes into account the diversity of training data. We hope that these ideas will stimulate further research on the base-decomposition technique and the general problem of large model compression. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, but there's a notable lack of research exploring the direct consequences of loss function changes. This study investigates how altering loss functions affects the performance of well-established classification neural networks. We're motivated by recent findings suggesting that, in some contexts, switching to a mislabelled sample resistant loss function like Kullback-Leibler can yield better results than traditional cross-entropy. However, our analysis reveals that applying this change is not universally advisable. This study aims to identify reliable loss function alternatives and establish guidelines for their use. To achieve this, we introduce a novel metric to assess the impact of loss function variation and examine the dependence of this metric on network architecture, data properties, and the target task. We also investigate the extent to which training dynamics are affected by loss function selection. Comprehensive experiments involving over 1 billion training steps were conducted to inform our analysis. The results of these experiments lead us to conclude that there's no single 'best' loss function and that selecting an optimal loss function is crucial. We also find that targeting the specific challenges of your particular training dataset is more important than choosing a loss function. Furthermore, our research indicates that the stability of training dynamics is a critical factor to consider when making loss function selections in the machine learning community. The code used in this study is publicly available at https://github.com/basilevh/Training- Dynamics. We hope this research will be useful to the deep learning community as a resource for making informed loss function choices. We're particularly interested in exploring the implications of our findings for multi-domain learning in future research. Additionally, we intend to expand on this study by developing a more sophisticated assessment of training dynamics that incorporates more detailed properties. We expect this increased detail will only serve to reinforce the importance of targeting the specific challenges of your particular training dataset. We're also interested in investigating the long-term consequences of loss function variation. We hypothesize that the relative superiority of different loss functions may become more apparent at the task level as the training period expands. We expect that future research will reveal loss functions with even greater potential than Kullback-Leibler, and that these loss functions will be especially effective when combined with large datasets. A new approach based on a perturbation theory is presented for the calculation of many-body interactions within a method called parquet theory. This method revolves around the decomposition of a four-point vertex into lower-order interactions. Through a transformation involving higher-order derivatives of the Hamiltonian, the parquet equations can be reinterpreted in terms of the Hamiltonian's eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. This perturbative parquet theory is capable of handling strong coupling regimes. A special case of the perturbative parquet theory, derived at second order, is equivalent to a well-known approach known as the vertex similarity renormalization group. Further, a perturbative parquet theory to any finite order is outlined. While this approach may retain solutions to the exact parquet equations for certain systems such as the two-dimensional Hubbard model at half filling, it necessarily becomes approximative for other systems. A related concept known as the Jarbass-Souma vertex is also reinterpreted as a perturbative parquet theory up to a specified order. Additionally, a perturbative parquet theory based on a functional derivative approach is presented and compared to a related approach using Lanczos lattices. Finally, a perturbative parquet theory is applied to study a system near a known transition in the two-dimensional Hubbard model where a novel phase with spinnon characteristics is believed to exist. In this study, a perturbative parquet theory up to the sixth order is employed to compute the free energy across this phase transition. Unlike other related approaches, this approach does not exhibit a singularity in the derivative of the free energy and is able to compute relevant quantities such as the spinon density in a certain regime. A related parquet theory known as the functional derivative parquet theory is also outlined and is capable of computing certain quantities as a power of a small parameter. In a special case where a certain parameter is set to zero, this approach is equivalent to a perturbative parquet theory based on higher derivatives of the Hamiltonian. Moreover, a functional derivative parquet theory is related to a family of solvable equations known as the functional renormalization group flow equations. A particular function known as the Wilson action is a solution to these equations that represents a perturbative parquet theory up to a specified order. Finally, a perturbative parquet theory is applied to a system where a strange metal is a possible phase and a phase transition from a normal metal to a topological insulator is studied. The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that restores symmetry by introducing a new order parameter. Well-known examples of exciton condensation include superconductivity and exciton-mediated pairing in ultra-cold gases, as well as the pressure-induced transformation in $\rm TiSe_2$. A computational method incorporating density-functional theory, many-body perturbation theory, and quantum Monte Carlo techniques can model the mechanism of exciton condensation. By applying this method to $\rm TiSe_2$, researchers have been able to demonstrate the role of strong electron-electron correlations in the phase transition and explain why it is necessary to go beyond a simple density-functional theory description. Furthermore, calculations using a new $ab ~initio$ technique confirm that $\rm TiSe_2$ undergoes a superconducting transition under high pressure due to the condensation of excitons. These findings also indicate the possibility of exciton condensation in other semimetals, potentially leading to novel quantum phases. A related prediction suggests that $\rm TiS_2$ could be driven into a quantum condensate of Majorana fermions under pressure. These research advancements mark an important milestone in the application of $ab ~initio$ techniques to the study of complex quantum phases and transitions. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on triplet Cooper pairs in a nematic superconductor, we developed a detailed model incorporating realistic materials characteristics and found that the magnetization response exhibits a paramagnetic component that is proportional to the square of the magnetic field. Through numerical calculations, we derived a general formula that describes the paramagnetic component and observed that in the case of s+ d nematic superconductors, this component is directly affected by the density of triplet Cooper pairs. Our findings also reveal that the magnetization response of triplet Cooper pairs is susceptible to a spin-precession phenomenon, resulting in a component that is proportional to the square root of the magnetic field. Furthermore, we observed that in s+ d nematic superconductors, this component is directly affected by the density of triplet Cooper pairs. On the other hand, in p+ d nematic superconductors, the magnetization response is primarily influenced by the polarization of triplet Cooper pairs rather than their density. Finally, we noted that the observed paramagnetic component may provide a viable mechanism for explaining experimental findings previously reported by researchers. Our study also highlights the distinct similarities and differences in magnetization responses between s+ d and p+ d nematic superconductors, which may provide a potential means of identifying and categorizing these materials. Our work further establishes that the proposed nematic superconducting models based on spin-triplet pairs are applicable and worthy of continued study.
