Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized 29 diverse prompts from sources such as politics, finance, commerce, technology, and education, and evaluated them using the superintendent dataset, which contains questions related to these domains. Our analysis of the relationship between prompt characteristics and performance identifies two predictors: (a) the average length of words, and (b) the variety of syllables within the prompt. Interestingly, higher prompt characteristics are associated with better results. Nonetheless, when we explored prompts from a semantic perspective by standardizing their subject matter and varying other aspects such as tone, it became apparent that some prompt types are inherently more effective. On the other hand, the variety of words and their sentiment do not predict zero-shot performance, suggesting that simpler prompts are more consistent. Our findings can guide the development of prompts in a manner that is both more systematic and transparent. The code and data used in this study are publicly available at https://github.com/jtrebuchy/Zero-Shot-Prompt-Analysis. Temporal data is inherent in various fields such as signal processing and speech recognition. Traditional deep learning techniques like convolutional networks are ineffective for temporal data analysis due to their lack of sequence awareness. In contrast, recurrent neural networks uniquely address the task of processing sequential information, making them an optimal choice for temporal data. This article delves into the principles and techniques of recurrent networks, especially those that can handle long-term dependencies, and discusses their applications in temporal data, including the challenging problem of temporal activity recognition where data often exhibits long, irregular patterns. A well-known method for handling such long-term dependencies is the long short-term memory network, and we will also explore other variants of LSTM as well as new architectures like transformer and distributed recurrent networks like factorized permanent neural networks. Finally, we will summarize the relevant parameters and implement exemplary experiments to compare these models in the context of temporal activity recognition. Ultimately, this article aims to provide a comprehensive guide to recurrent neural networks and establish the foundations for future research in this area. In particular, we assume the reader is familiar with basic neural network concepts, linear regression, and the backpropagation algorithm. We investigate how timely decisions to implement non-pharmaceutical measures impact both the extent of outbreak damage and the resulting economic loss, and discover that a specific strategy, involving proportionate closures of social venues, yields an 'optimal' outcome – one size fits all solution that minimizes both health and economic losses. We find that the degree of economic loss is directly related to the effective reproduction number, and reveal that a one-size-fits-all strategy actually corresponds to maintaining an 'effective' reproduction number of approximately 1, representing a temporary, pandemic-specific exception to the rule. Our analysis also uncovers a fundamental connection between the average and marginal economic loss, and highlights the significance of timely interventions, as delaying such decisions leads to greater damage and loss. To facilitate our analysis, we introduce three simple, fundamental methods to model pandemic mitigation, and provide an easily accessible framework for policymakers to make data-driven decisions, even when limited information is available. The process of verifying machine learning model output quality relies heavily on examining individual training dataset samples and attributing predicted outcomes. However, traditional sensitivity analysis is inadequate in a data-driven exploration, especially when relying on models such as deep neural networks, as it struggles to determine how sample characteristics affect class probabilities on a dataset level. A possible solution is to apply the Shapley value formula, already investigated in the context of explaining individual predictions and feature importance, to operate on a dataset basis. Despite its potential, a significant barrier stands in the way - the enormous computational cost of applying the approach to a large dataset. This hurdle can be overcome by generating a subset of the dataset that is deemed "significant" according to the Shapley value method, which is capable of capturing the dependencies within a dataset with a much lower number of samples. The proposed significant subset can then be used for data debugging purposes, such as identifying data patterns or diagnosing classification difficulties. The approach is developed and tested within the context of an end-to-end machine learning pipeline based on Python and the KubeFlow framework. Its performance is evaluated using the Federated Learning benchmark and the ImageNet dataset. The proposed debugging methodology is compared to alternative techniques, such as data augmentation and debugging in an active learning setting. The experiments demonstrate that Shapley significance yields a compact and interpretable dataset subset that effectively captures important data patterns, enabling debugging and dataset pruning with a much lower number of samples compared to traditional approaches. The corresponding code is available for reproduction of the results at https://github.com/maksimov-ir/shapley-significance. A pressurable trimerization transformation offers an alternative means to control the arrangement of spins in materials, presenting a distinct mechanism for regulating physical properties. This concept is exemplified in manganese trihalides, where trimerization within the planar $ab$-plane induces an inverse anomalous Hall effect due to the presence of skew-local spin currents originating from the structural symmetry breaking. When this trimerization is hydrostatically compressed into a single domain, it transforms into an $A$-type antiferromagnet, causing the anomalous Hall effect to cease. Conversely, returning the pressure to a multi-domain state reinitiates the effect; thus, pressure-regulated trimerization may be a viable means to control the anomalous Hall effect in these materials. This discovery could provide new avenues for researching spin-dependent transport properties in materials with complex spin arrangements. Research on these types of materials, such as Mn$_3$Sn, using multi-instrumentation, has confirmed these properties and provided comprehensive characterization. Utilizing high-pressure X-ray diffraction, the structural transformations within the material were studied in real-time. Subsequent experiments involving transport, magnetization, and Hall measurements under varying pressures demonstrated that a single-domain state of the antiferromagnet leads to the disappearance of the anomalous Hall effect. This phenomenon presents a unique case in research on magnetism-driven anomalous Hall effect phenomena. Improving the accuracy of outcome prediction in cancer patients is a primary goal for which risk prediction models based on cancer subnetworks have been developed. However, these models face the challenge of underlying network complexity, which cannot be adequately represented by traditional graph models. This issue is addressed through the use of hypergraphs to represent interactions between multiple nodes in complex networks. Although hypergraphs offer this representation capability, their large number of dimensions poses a limitation, making it difficult to apply to large-scale biological networks such as those involved in cancer. To address this limitation, a guided hypergraph reconstruction framework is presented that reduces the number of dimensions needed to describe the network, while maintaining the ability to represent important guidelines such as cell cycle progression. The framework uses a combination of mutation and expression data to determine optimal reconstruction parameters and evaluates its performance through comparison with previous methods, ultimately achieving more accurate outcome prediction results. The implementation of this framework is provided through a package called GHRR, which includes code and data examples to support its use in practical applications. This work presents a novel approach to guided hypergraph reconstruction that enables accurate prediction of cancer outcomes, while providing a framework for further research and development in network-based cancer therapy. In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data,
typically obtained via MRI, CT, or X-ray technologies. However, translating raw
imagery into clinical language is challenging. To overcome this difficulty, we've
created detailed annotations of chest X-rays by simulating MRI or CT scans,
enabling us to project them onto two-dimensional X-ray images. This technique
facilitates machine learning model development for radiology report generation.
Furthermore, our dataset is augmented with cardiac bounding box annotations,
enabling models to recognize and describe the heart's position relative to the
torso. Our annotation process is demonstrated to yield radiology reports that
correlate strongly with actual doctor-generated reports, according to multiple
evaluation metrics. Moreover, our approach empowers machines to provide more
detailed and accurate descriptions of the heart and lungs, surpassing current
ablations. Finally, our models, along with the associated code and annotations,
are open-source, allowing other researchers to build upon our findings. We
anticipate that our models will contribute to developing more informative and
accurate medical imaging reports. In addition to paper link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.14209. Model and dataset are available at this link: https://github.com/FCPPII/RAD-report-generation. Our research addresses how stable the value of cryptocurrencies is as a medium of exchange by comparing their price fluctuations to those of conventional currencies. We discovered that most cryptocurrencies experience price variations of 10% or more in a single day, significantly differing from the 3-4% daily price changes of major conventional currencies like the US dollar or the euro. This substantial difference in price stability thresholds distinguishes cryptocurrencies from conventional currencies, implying that their current usage primarily aligns with investment rather than everyday exchange purposes. To facilitate their adoption as a medium of exchange, cryptocurrencies must first demonstrate the ability to maintain relatively stable values relative to traditional currencies. We found that one way to achieve this is by reducing their daily price variation rate relative to major currencies. Another potential approach is by decreasing the time interval used to measure price stability, as this results in more stable values for cryptocurrencies relative to major currencies. Nonetheless, achieving stability at smaller time intervals may not be sufficient to justify using cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. In addition to analyzing price stability, we also assessed the relationship between the value of cryptocurrencies and various cryptocurrency-specific factors, discovering that their price often correlates with factors like the total number of cryptocurrency transactions, but not consistently with factors like the percentage of cryptocurrency users or the operating status of cryptocurrency nodes. Moreover, we found no consistent evidence that the price of cryptocurrencies is linked to conventional macroeconomic variables. While some regression analyses indicated slight correlations, these results were not consistent and did not hold up across all cryptocurrencies. In contrast, we found that price relationships exist among different cryptocurrencies, as well as between cryptocurrencies and gold, reflecting their shared status as investment assets. To further explore the links between cryptocurrency prices, we analyzed their relationships with time-series models that use macroeconomic variables, discovering that these models often fail to accurately forecast cryptocurrency prices as they are based on conventional economic assumptions that do not apply to cryptocurrencies. Notably, while some regression analyses indicated nearly perfect fit in terms of r-squared values, the actual forecast errors were significant, demonstrating the limitations of conventional economic models for predicting cryptocurrency prices. In contrast, more advanced machine learning approaches may be more effective at forecasting cryptocurrency prices, but their performance also varies depending on the specific model used and the time period being predicted. In general, our research found that forecasting cryptocurrency prices is challenging, especially when compared to conventional currencies, due to their extreme price variability and lack of correlation with traditional macroeconomic variables. A novel defect identification approach for patterned fabric images is proposed, 
utilizing a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, in conjunction with 
low-rath decomposition to effectively classify defects. Owing to the unique 
directional structure of fabrics, traditional feature detectors commonly used 
in computer vision prove inadequate for fabric defect detection. This shortfall 
has been mitigated by the development of the GHOG descriptor, which integrates 
directional derivative information into the Horizontal-Vertical-Oriented Gradients 
feature, resulting in an expanded directional space. The incorporation of this 
directional space into the widely-established SIFT algorithm has been shown to 
improve the performance of basic SIFT for fabric defect detection. Follow-up 
research involved refining this technique by dividing the image into sub-bands 
based on dominant fabric patterns and applying the GHOG descriptor to each, 
which enables more precise extraction of directional features. Ultimately, the 
most distinct directional features are fused to create a low-rank decomposition 
based directional feature descriptor, effectively capturing the global directional 
structure of fabric images. The resulting descriptor has been successfully 
implemented in a neural network for defect identification, yielding commendable 
results and establishing a robust foundation for more intricate deep learning

Intelligent systems that interact with their environment are increasingly requiring skills like visual tracking and navigation. Traditional methods rely on pre-programmed instructions, but this approach is impractical for complex tasks, so we turn to reinforcement learning as a more realistic solution. By incorporating a data-driven component into the skill acquisition process, reinforcement learning allows for the development of more adaptable and effective algorithms. However, without sufficient regularization, overfitting can occur when learning from imperfect or limited data, which can cause these algorithms to focus on irrelevant details in the input data. To address this issue, we explore the use of information-theoretic regularization, which helps the agent optimize its behavior while also making efficient use of available data. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we designed a simulation environment that mimics the challenge of visual guidance, where a robot must navigate to a target through a distance that is measured visually. The observation space includes noisy and varied visual data, making this task suitable for testing our approach. When compared to existing reinforcement learning methods, our results show that the proposed approach, which utilizes information-theoretic regularization, delivers a more efficient and accurate learning process, with a notable increase in training samples required to achieve a certain level of performance. This is an achievable cost, as the differences in final agent performance are minimal. Furthermore, the trained agents using the proposed approach exhibit more flexible and adaptable behavior, as evidenced by their ability to handle out-of-distribution data and target changes. Overall, the incorporation of information-theoretic regularization facilitates more accurate and efficient skill acquisition through reinforcement learning. We provide a comprehensive description of quadrics within the context of categorical geometry by establishing a one-to-one relationship between certain categories and quadrics in projective spaces. Specifically, our results relate the category of finite-dimensional hermitian forms over a commutative ring to the quadrics in a projective space constructed using that ring's bilinear forms. This categorification offers an abstract representation of quadrics, which enables the study of morphism spaces between quadrics through the use of category theory. Moreover, it enables the development of a homological algebra for quadrics and facilitates the investigation of fibre products and other universal constructs in this context. The evidence for our claims consists of a series of detailed diagrams illustrating the categories and quadrics involved. Ultimately, this framework is poised to provide a suitable ground for generalising quadrics to arbitrary algebraic geometries. Our approach is inspired by the established theories of projective algebra and projective trigonometry. As such, the proposed generalisation should be compatible with these existing theories. Furthermore, this framework is anticipated to be closely linked with the category of hermitian forms, which is a key component of k-theory. Specifically, it is expected to play a pivotal role in the pending proof of the k-theoretic generalisation of the euler-poincare formula for arithmetic quadrics. Additionally, this framework is anticipated to be a crucial component in the ongoing development of a projective description of motives. The proposed categorification of quadrics should also serve as a prototype for generalising arbitrary algebraic geometric objects and, ultimately, for extending this process to topological and noncommutative quadrics. Lastly, this framework is expected to provide fresh insights into the classical quadrics that have already been studied for so long. Specifically, it is anticipated that category theory will shed a new and interesting light on the projective algebra, projective linear algebra and projective trigonometry that have been explored in such great detail. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our research includes a comprehensive set of benchmarks that not only evaluate the performance of virtual agents but also their creators, offering a unified framework to compare them.
Our study showcases the benefits of accelerating text-based games, enabling a notable breakthrough in agent performance, and reveals intriguing connections between processing speed and agent design that would have gone unnoticed in lower processing speeds. 
Finally, we outline potential applications of TextWorldExpress, ranging from fine-tuning agent technologies to simulating the behavior of future advanced agents. 
The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Orion-PM/textworldexpress. 
It requires the PyTextGame framework also openly available at https://github.com/Orion-PM/PyTextGame. Le and Wang (2021).

The way robots move and grasp objects is typically controlled and planned in a linear space, but in reality, this is similar to trying to predict the weather using only today's temperature to forecast the weather five days from now - it just doesn't give an accurate result. To get around this limitation, researchers have come up with a new method for planning robot movements that takes into account the underlying, curved structure of the robot's manipulability space, which represents its possible motions and grasps. This structure is particularly important in tasks like object manipulation, where the robot needs to move along a curved path to execute a successful maneuver. However, representing and navigating these curves is challenging due to the lack of suitable numerical methods. To overcome this, we've developed two key techniques: one allows us to map complex, curved structures onto simpler linear spaces, where it's easier to plan; and another, specialized algorithm that helps the robot match its expected manipulability patterns with the actual ones by efficiently aligning corresponding structures, even when there are obstacles and other distortions in its environment. We've successfully tested these new methods on complex 3D objects and demonstrated that they outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques. This new approach means the robot can now plan its movements more accurately along the optimal, curved paths that are best suited for a successful grasp. As a result, its chances of successfully executing the grasp increase, which is a crucial metric for measuring its manipulability space. This method has been successfully implemented and is now available for evaluation on the CASPER robot platform. It has also been developed as a part of the CU-RO robot platform's manipulability tool, which is based on the ROS2 distribution. This tool is designed to make the robot's manipulability space more accessible and easy to work with. By doing so, it enables researchers to develop more advanced, curved-motion planning strategies, which could lead to significant breakthroughs in a wide range of robotic tasks. This includes not only object manipulation, but also other complex tasks like navigating through tight spaces and performing high-precision, curved-motion maneuvers to execute a successful grasp. With this new approach, these tasks become much easier to perform. This work is a significant advancement in this area and represents a major contribution to the field. It has also been influenced by the human motor control system, which uses a variety of numerical methods to plan its own curvilinear motion patterns along the manipulability space. As a result, this method is expected to lead to more similar and robust robotic motion

We develop a theoretical approach for controlling the intensity and wavelength of attosecond pulses generated through high-field coherent transition momentum mechanisms. By considering a two-color field from a laser and a free-electron oscillator, we establish that manipulating laser parameters leads to adjustable attosecond pulse patterns. These pulses can be fine-tuned in duration, wavelength, and intensity using a cross talk between two colors, resulting in a controllable, wide-range spectrum. This framework offers a new approach to achieving the highly coherent, high-intensity pulses needed for breakthroughs in attosecond science and fast electron imaging. Furthermore, it provides a crucial connection between attosecond pulse generation and advanced irradiation techniques, potentially expanding the scope of strong-field laser physics to include new areas of research. We suggest that in experiments using both linearly polarized and circularly polarized lasers, one-color and multi-color setups could generate distinctive attosecond pulse patterns, thereby expanding the scope of strong-field laser physics and achieving highly coherent, high-intensity pulses. These pulse patterns could be modified through changes in laser parameters, enabling the creation of adjustable attosecond pulses that are incredibly short in duration, have a high intensity, or cover a broad range of wavelengths. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that it may be possible to achieve attosecond pulse durations that are comparable to the electron motion period itself, potentially leading to a new frontier in attosecond science and fast electron imaging, along with a deeper understanding of highly charged electron interactions. Lastly, we note that attosecond pulse generation may also be developed using table-top Petawatt lasers and free-electron lasers in the future. This paper investigates explosion solutions, or solutions with non-integrable integrals at a specific point, for the Schrödinger equation in free space, particularly when coupled with a nonlinear term that includes exponential and power-law components. We demonstrate that under specific conditions including a nonlinear exponent greater than one, there are no explosion solutions that avoid the origin. Additionally, solutions that encounter an obstacle in the form of a convex region fall under the same category as those in free space due to the development of a well-defined "interface" near the obstacle, effectively acting as a barrier to contain the explosion. In contrast, solutions with lower nonlinear exponents greater than or equal to zero exhibit unique properties and interactions with the obstacle in the form of a trapped or localized energy behavior. Notably, solutions with negative $H^{1}_{\infty}$ norms in the $L^2$ space can occur and are confined to the obstacle's influence, leading to the definition of a new interface and property criterion. Finally, solutions exhibit a critical value at $l=1/2$, marking the boundary between these new properties and the behaviors observed in free space or near a obstacle. We support these findings with well-normalized and well-located estimates of the solutions and their derivatives, emphasizing the solution's structure near the obstacle and its interaction with the Schrödinger equation's nonlinear component. As a result, this work provides insight into solutions' behaviors and their relationship to the equation's well-posedness and the solutions' non-uniqueness in various scenarios. Moreover, this research offers a mathematical confirmation and extension of the solutions' non-uniqueness, which was previously demonstrated under weaker condition on the nonlinearity exponent as well as the non-existence of certain singular solutions, including the zero solution with a strong singularity. Finally, this work remains incomplete, leaving room for potential future research in this area. We hypothesize an additional criterion $l<1/2$ may be required for unique well-posed solutions and leave its verification for future investigation. We also briefly discuss some interesting physical implications of these mathematical findings. We anticipate these results will contribute to a deeper understanding of the solutions and their properties, bridging the gap between physical and mathematical inferences. We also note that these results are contingent on the obstacle being a convex domain, and we leave the exploration of various types of non-convex obstacles for future research. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of modal logic to the topological properties of specific categories. Building on similar work done by Lawvere and Johnson, we expand on this concept while making it more accessible to the logical community. This approach allows us to establish a universal system that can represent various types of modal logic within a consistent framework. 

In this first part of a two-paper series, we focus on setting up the foundational elements of this framework, whereas the second paper will delve into more specific applications and examples. This framework has natural inclusions for the composition of modal logics and the interaction of modal logics with topological structures. It also enables the formation of products, sums, and quotients for modal logics. Furthermore, this framework provides a unified system for modal logics based on substructural mules. 

We have also set up a system that allows for the automatic translation of modal correspondence results into the context of topological categories. This approach is demonstrated through the translation of the Sahlqvist correspondence theorem. This paper also lays the groundwork for a general methodology to study modal logics through the topological categories framework. This will be further utilized in the second paper where we apply this approach to specific modal logics. This translation also enables us to devise a natural modal logic interpretation of the Sanz-Sese framework for modal logic. 

In this first part of the paper, we have also defined a concept called modalizability and used it to show that modal logics based on substructural mules are modalizably equivalent if and only if their corresponding topological categories are subquotient equivalent. This reveals that the notion of modalizability is a categorical analogue of the notion of subquotient. This provides a new perspective on the relationship between modal logics and their topological categories.

This paper examines the resolution of an inverse problem involving expensive computer simulations that generate time series data, by modeling the output of these simulations as continuous functions on specific domains. By applying a parameter estimation technique called Multi-Contour Estimation (MCE), which is an optimization method rooted in evolutionary algorithms, researchers can constrain the search for input parameters using series of output profiles, obtained through costly computer simulations, to narrow down the parameter space. This multi-objective optimization approach is proven to be efficient and capable of handling expensive computer simulations, by limiting the number of output profiles needed, as demonstrated through a practical study of solving an inverse problem in fluid dynamics. By comparing the proposed method with other optimization techniques such as Multi-Objective Evolutionary Programming (MOEP), Parametric Reduced-Optimization Benchmark (PRORB), and a classical optimization method rooted in quasi-Newton, researchers found that MCE significantly reduces the computational cost associated with these approaches, while still obtaining accurate results for the input parameters. In particular, MCE requires only about 2 to 20 output profiles, in contrast to other optimization methods that need up to 16,000 profiles to obtain similar results. This significant reduction in computational cost is attributed to the constraint-based search strategy used in MCE, which enables the efficient identification of promising regions of the parameter space. $\mathcal{C}$-Optimization, a variant of the PRORB method, also showed excellent results, while being computationally more economical than other optimization methods. However, further research is needed to investigate its performance on a wider range of problems. In terms of the quality of the estimated profiles, MCE performed best, with a small margin over other optimization methods. Notably, the proposed method 1) avoids evaluating the computer simulator at unnecessary points, thus reducing its computational cost; 2) provides a tight fit to the feasible region without using any post-optimization processing; and 3) facilitates the estimation of input profiles with a small margin of error. In addition to these key advantages, MCE also demonstrated excellent results in terms of the number of output profiles required (two to 20) and the distribution of these profiles, which was concentrated and easy to interpret. This concentration of output profiles is a direct result of the search strategy used in MCE and its ability to efficiently identify the optimal region of the parameter space. Therefore, MCE not only reduces the computational cost associated with the output profiles but also provides a more transparent and understandable search strategy. Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using colorless MZFs, we now show that alternating versions require colored MZFs. This is demonstrated by deriving a colored MFZF formula for $\sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} L_{m,k} \zeta^{m+1}(1+\cdots + 1)$, where $L_{m,k}$ is defined as $2^{\underline{m}} \prod_{j=0}^{m-1} (1-j) / (1+2+\cdots + (m-1)k)$. As a by-product, we also obtain a colored MFZF formula for $\sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} L_{m,k} \zeta^{m+1}(1+\cdots + 1+2+ \cdots + (m-1)k)$. This result is an extension of an earlier finding by the same authors. To validate our new formula, we also derive a corresponding Apéry-type series with summation indices of mixed parities. This is achieved by combining a recent series expansion of the Hurwitz zeta function, specifically $\zeta(s+1,n+1)$, which we call the "five-parameter" zeta function, with a combination of colorless and colored MZFs. This new formula enables the computation of various inverse binomial series involving powers of $\sqrt{2}$ and solutions to the related problem of Apéry-type. Finally, we also express the same series as a sum of two alternating Apéry-type series with a new, simpler series involving only $\zeta(s+1,2)$ as a by-product. This is a notable improvement, as this new series has a new denumerator, shifting the previous 'irrelevant' poles into the numerator and thus eliminating the related transcendental constants. This is a significant finding, as it means the associated values are now log-concave. As before, we also obtain a corresponding series involving powers of $\sqrt{2}$. All of these results are the first of their kind. Finally, we also point out that, although all of these results are new, some of them can be obtained with a different approach using only colorless MZFs.

The materials were pressed into shapes at various levels of heat and then fired at temperatures between 900 and 1200 degrees Celsius to analyze their internal structure and compressive strength. The experiment demonstrated that moldable substances could be used to construct structures on other planets, paving the way for future development of habitats on Mars and the Moon. When a fiber is immersed in a liquid and covered with a drop, the interaction between the liquid and the fiber leads to a new droplet forming around the fiber. This new droplet can then undergo an Rayleigh-Plateau instability, resulting in which the liquid forms into spherical caps and eventually falls off the fiber due to the growth of waves. This acceleration is a result of reduced viscosity and increased pressure due to the movement of the liquid, causing the liquid to be more easily expelled from the fiber. By using far-infrared and sub-millimeter observations, researchers can directly assess dust emission associated with star formation activities, yet its interpretation is complicated by limitations in modeling current space telescopes and observations.  We analyze the reliability of using SPED fitting to estimate star formation rates (SFR) by comparing it with far-infrared luminosity, a established method.  This study employs  303 local galaxies with comprehensive data from the Spitzer Infrared Spectrometer For Space Exploration (SIRS) legacy project, featuring high signal-to noise ratios for an accurate comparison.  By examining these galaxies using the PRODIGY code, we determine that the star formation rates are directly proportional to far-infrared luminosity, with a typical scatter of 0.2 mag.  We identify the basis for this linear relationship as the consistent correlation between starlight attenuation and dust emission across various galaxy masses.  Furthermore, we determine that the average conversion factor of SFR is 1.21 times $L_{FIR}/10^{9}L_{\odot}$ or, equivalently, 2.05 times $L_{28\mu m}/10^{28}erg~s^{-1}~cm^{-2}$.  We develop an empirical formula to predict the extinction-free SFR based solely on optical data and, in addition, propose an updated approach to deriving star formation rates by combining far-infrared and optical observations, featuring a reduced scatter of 0.13 mag.  This method presents an alternative solution to the complex problem of estimating star formation rates by fitting galaxy spectra, providing an easily applicable solution for the broad astrophysics community.  In addition, we apply the proposed approach to assess the dark matter content in galaxies, with an associated reduction in uncertainty. We present a novel solution to the general diffusion equation, applicable to any initial conditions and diffusion coefficient. The method employs a special system of first-order partial differential equations that can be solved using a variety of numerical methods, such as those already established in existing literature. We demonstrate that our approach can be extended to the multi-dimensional case and even tackle situations with time-dependent boundaries, offering a versatile framework for diffusion-related applications. Furthermore, we provide a set of numerical experiments that showcase the method's effectiveness. We found that our approach performs similarly to existing methods but offers enhanced flexibility, making it a valuable general-purpose tool for diffusion equations. The corresponding code is available for review on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/tiepengchen/general_diffusion/tree/main. Additionally, a standalone code for our method is available under the name 'general_diffusion.py' within the repository. We also generated a pair of Python packages, 'pdqtools' and 'fdqtools', that contain classes for solving diffusion equations through the methods described in Sections 3.1 and 3.2, respectively, as well as other related problems, which can be installed via pip using the following command: `pip install pdqtools fdqtools`. We have also generated a series of educational modules, 'diffcounter', that contain specific tools for counting particles in certain regions during simulations of diffusion, which can be installed via pip using the command `pip install diffcounter`. We are planning to significantly expand the capabilities of 'diffcounter' to encompass more general diffusion applications. We believe this will be a comprehensive and user-friendly tool for particle simulation and will be made available under a permissive open-source license. This work presents an innovative approach to recognize handwritten mathematical expressions in depth sensor data. The proposed system is composed of two main modules: a module that converts raw data to polynomial expressions and a detection module. The polynomial generation module leverages machine learning and SIFT descriptors to convert raw data into polynomial expressions, representing 3D spatial relationships between key points. The detection module, trained with polynomial expressions from the CME dataset, employs a nearest neighbor search method to determine the correct handwritten mathematical expression. The effectiveness of the proposed system was evaluated through experiments involving polynomial based representations and raw data, demonstrating its superiority to existing methods under specific conditions. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in speech synthesis by employing non-parametric approaches. Instead of relying on a specific distribution to create synthetic durations, our approach uses a median-based method. It implies that each pair of adjacent speech units in a database generates a synthetic duration with equal probability. This non-parametric approach is more flexible and efficient than traditional methods, requiring less data and resulting in lower variances when estimating durations. Moreover, it enables the creation of unique synthetic durations for any speech sequence, whereas, in contrast, methods relying on parametric distributions may struggle to generate durations for very long sequences due to the challenge of filling in gaps in the distribution function for long sequences. This non-parametric approach is similar to the effective technique used in language modelling, which is called katib. This method has successfully been used in the NAOSS speech synthesis system and has led to improvements in its speech duration modelling. Experiments have confirmed that the non-parametric approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art duration modelling technique used in the NAOSS system. Moreover, the system based on this non-parametric approach achieved high quality scores in objective tests, demonstrating its effectiveness for speech synthesis duration modelling. Code for this approach is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/advance-speech/median-duration-model. Additionally, the corresponding pre-trained models can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/advance-speech/naoss-models. Moreover, the speech synthesis system used in this study is also available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/advance-speech/naoss-system. To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Gaussian process prior. This model addresses two key issues: it uses an unsupervised method to learn the intrinsic variability of SN Ia spectra, and employs a targeted dimensionality reduction that preserves essential spectral features. Our results show that the model effectively captures the intrinsic variability of SN Ia spectra with a limited number of features, and demonstrates the significance of including a GP prior in the encoder. Furthermore, we found that the model performs better than other well-known methods such as PCA and AE, particularly in extracting essential features from degraded spectral data. Using the trained model, we generated synthetic temporal series that are comparable to real data, and observed feature evolution patterns similar to those found in the actual data. These synthetic data can be used as mock observations for testing future SNS data analysis methods. Additionally, we developed a technique to analyze the contributed feature spaces of SNS Ia spectra, and found that the features captured by the model are associated with specific feature spaces that are sensitive to electron temperature and gravity. This is a novel finding, and indicates that the model could be used to provide additional constraints on the physical conditions of SN Ia explosions. The influence of light and self-weighting particles on turbulent plumes is examined, with specific focus on how these particles affect the plume's vertical velocity and direction. Numerical modeling reveals that light particles enhance the vertical velocity near the base of the plume, whereas heavy particles have an opposite effect. This is because light particles gather in the plume's initial stages, creating a reservoir of high vertical velocity. In contrast, heavy particles settle at the base of the grid, exerting drag on the plume and reducing the vertical velocity. Moreover, the plume's direction is influenced by particles as they absorb and emit heat, causing asymmetry that may lead to loop formations. This study demonstrates that the plume's properties are sensitive to the average size and weight of its particles. A representative example is given for a plume filled with sulfur particles in a 10-meter-tall tank, illustrating the impact of particles on the vertical velocity and direction. This research also highlights the potential of particle-filled plumes to influence geochemical and geophysical processes in the Earth's near surface. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals the interplay between network structure and disease dynamics. However, as the disease model becomes more complex, so does the required network topology for the avoidance of epidemics. In two dimensions, this topological criterion is essentially the planar nature of the network, allowing for the application of mathematical techniques, like complex analysis, to analyze the problem. Nevertheless, as we explore more complex network topologies, such as hypergraphs, the ability to use similar mathematical approaches fails, and a different methodology is needed to solve the problem. By employing an entirely new method based on the weakly Riemannian structure and the $\bar{\partial}$-operator, we are able to derive a spectral condition for the non-existence of epidemics in hypergraphs and establish a general theorem for this scenario. As a direct application of our spectral approach, we are able to determine the critical threshold for the survival of an immunized population within a hypergraph structure. Ultimately, this research seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for the extinction vs. survival analysis of epidemics within various network topologies, starting with hypergraphs as a pioneering case. Additionally, we introduce an algorithm to find the non-existence spectrum of an epidemic on a given hypergraph. Furthermore, we derive an approximation formula for the edge and net out-degrees distributions in hypergraphs. By analyzing the distribution of out-degrees in a hypergraph, and comparing it to that of a corresponding complete graph, which corresponds to a model for epidemics, we find that the difference in their spectral behavior leads to an inequality that could be useful in analyzing the behavior of epidemics on hypergraphs. This research also introduces ratio theorems for the spectrum of an epidemic on a hypergraph, analogous to similar theorems for the spectrum of a graph, and concludes by introducing numerous problems for further investigation. Finally, we illustrate our theoretical findings with the help of numerous numerical examples. This study examines how rotation affects the output of solar-type dynamo models when placed in an anti-solar rotation profile, where the differential rotation increases with the radial distance. By combining a rotating convection zone with a non-rotating or slowly rotating tachocline, the models generate magnetic fields through a dynamo process. As the differential rotation increases with radius, the models experience a shift in the rotation balance, leading to shorter lifetimes and decreased activity levels. For anti-solar differential rotation, the models exhibit cyclic behavior only when the rotation rate in the convective zone is relatively low. However, the cyclic patterns disappear or become less stable as the rotation rate in the convective zone increases. To maintain cyclic solutions, the angular momentum flux due to turbulent diffusion must be reduced. The results of this study suggest that it may be challenging for stars with rapid differential rotation to enter a state of low activity similar to the Sun's "anti-solar" phase. The dynamic quenching mechanism in these dynamos is significantly affected by the violent turbulent transport of angular momentum that occurs in rapidly rotating regions. The dynamic quenching mechanism is reduced or cannot explain the disappearance of cyclic solutions for strongly rotating cases. The quasi-geostrophic dynamo cannot provide solutions for rapidly rotating cases. Additionally, the anti-solar differential rotation cases are less efficient than the torsional oscillation cases. The solar-type dynamo that operates solely in the convective zone is not capable of producing cyclic solutions, especially those with prolonged duration, due to its inability to generate magnetic fields in the tachocline. We introduce McMini, a novel model checker designed for verifying the correctness of multithreaded programs. Leveraging a disk-access-efficient data structure, McMini employs a partitioned memory representation to enhance performance. It integrates a McMini interpreter, enabling seamless transition between high-level source code and model-checking tools. As a DPOR-based model checker, McMini facilitates efficient detection of thread-parallel executions and allows for a wide range of flexibility through the addition of side-effect-free actions. Furthermore, McMini's McMini-check framework serves as a versatile tool for creating custom model-checking tools by incorporating various action types, including McMini/check, a specific tool with built-in atomic mc-minis. We evaluate McMini using a diverse set of 29 benchmark programs, showcasing its effectiveness and practical value as a model checker. It outperforms or matches existing model checkers in various scenarios, with particular success in verifying program regions with multiple threads accessing shared memory in a hierarchical structure. However, it exhibits performance limitations when compared to McMini/check, a more optimized tool designed for specific program patterns. Through this work, we contribute three key areas: (i) McMini, a general-purpose model checker, (ii) a novel performance-enhancing McMini/check tool, and (iii) 29 benchmark programs, including 8 new mc-mini-specific benchmarks, that enable quantitative performance evaluations across various scenarios. Specifically, we concentrate on one-loop corrections, suppressing higher-loop terms due to the principle of perturbative decoupling. Our results are exemplified through two composite models: a Dirac-Gauss-Bonnet term and a pseudo-Goldstone boson. The features of BICEP2 can be reproduced in both scenarios, where a heavy scalar is involved in breaking supersymmetry. We obtain novel estimates for the number of Borel sets in various partitions of the real line, utilizing measure-theoretic and probabilistic arguments that often involve comparing random functions with continuous ones on the real axis. These estimates demonstrate that different partition methods have vastly different cardinalities, with some Borel partitions being at least $\mathfrak{c}$ larger than others. To confirm this, we construct an explicit homeomorphism between two types of Borel set partitions, proving that one partition is at least continuously enumerable in terms of the other. Furthermore, we show that another partition is countably enumerable in terms of Lebesgue measure, resolving an open problem from 2003. In the 2000s, a significant shift occurred in the US investment industry, from a dominant top-down approach to a more widespread use of bottom-up fundamental analysis. A new wave of agent-based models aims to explain this transformation, suggesting that a new type of investment tactic emerged, facilitating the survival of fundamental analysis in the face of opposing pressures from value and growth styles. We examine the critical underlying parameters of these models, arguing that they are often chosen with a particular outcome in mind, instead of being an accurate depiction of the initial conditions. We propose that the challenge of modeling the dynamic interaction of different investment tactics, characteristic of the US experience, requires careful consideration of the method of representation, especially when using binary representations. Our study illustrates this complexity, showing that the success of a new tactic doesn't necessarily imply the failure of existing ones. Its implications are significant, also covering the coexistence of different research methods in financial economics. Moreover, our findings highlight the significance of carefully establishing the initial context of a research question in order to avoid unintended consequences. Although our analysis is grounded in the recent US investment history, the general principles of agent-based models and the specific case study also render it relevant to the current COVID-19 pandemic. Finally, we suggest that the binary approach of many agent-based models might not be sufficiently sophisticated to address complex phenomena, such as the current US investment landscape. In the long term, a more nuanced representation might be required to thoroughly explain the dynamic interaction of different investment tactics. Given the novel context of the pandemic and the'stay-at-home' measures, this need for a more refined model becomes particularly pronounced. In addition to presenting our theoretical analysis, we also provide a supplementary document containing a more detailed description of the empirical research and the results of two complementary experiments. These additional findings are motivated by the recent COVID-19 pandemic and the resulting'stay-at-home' measures, creating a novel context. As the investment industry is likely to be affected by this event in various ways, it presents an intriguing case study of the agent-based models. Moreover, the supplementary document contains two complementary experiments that explore the influence of two distinct phenomena - the stock market's information capacity and the social connections among fund managers. These additional analyses provide a more comprehensive understanding of the agent-based models, also covering the survival of fundamental analysis during the pandemic. A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerging from unseen data patterns on various devices can impede this technique as they are not accessible to the central server or fellow users. We design a unified federated learning framework to conquer this obstacle by omitting the requirement that all users must be familiar with the comprehensive class set. Instead, we allow users to transmit information regarding their unique classes in a encrypted manner. By having these surfaces redirect reflector-signal paths, we can dynamically adjust the channels and potentially boost data transfer rates. However, this feature introduces a highly complex multi-path environment that must be overcome by developing an efficient algorithm for uplink channel estimation. Our proposed solution involves employing a least-squares-based approach with a data-compression technique to minimize the number of messages exchanged between users and the base station. Furthermore, we investigate the performance of our algorithm and compare it to a benchmark solution with optimal performance, but higher computational complexity. Our simulation results indicate that the new algorithm offers an optimal balance between computational simplicity and performance. This study analyzes data from a national survey of 450 local news websites across the U.S., examining variations in coverage of the pandemic among news outlets and their relationships with community-level COVID cases and deaths, as well as audience sizes. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter to support the retrieval of multiple sets. We introduce a new modification, the XOR filter, which is an adaptation of this concept. The XOR filter can be used as a member of several sets of filters, each of which identifies a distinct set. It offers a combination of the efficiency of Bloom and cuckoo filters, making it suitable for a wide range of tasks. If designed carefully, the XOR filter can match the performance of the best available solutions while providing more flexibility than needed in many cases. We also introduce three novel algorithms for managing a group of filters, called a filter bank, that are more efficient than previous options. These algorithms, which are part of a general framework for managing filter banks, are based on the use of XOR filters. They are used to solve two other problems: managing a group of arrays and approximating the retrieval of multiple values in a sequence. The first problem is similar to the issue of removing duplicates in a list while maintaining the order of the items. The second problem is a variation of the issue of finding the first occurrence of a value in a sequence. The solutions to these problems are often used as pre-processing actions for more complex tasks, such as counting the occurrences of values in a sequence or validating whether a sequence is within a set of allowed sequences. The identification of super-Earths and sub-Neptunes has led to a renewed drive to understand the basic components and processes of these exoplanets. Solubility equilibrium and gas thermochemistry are two key mechanisms that shape a planet's composition, influencing which gases are released into its atmosphere during the liquidification of its core. We explore the distinguishable signs of these processes that can be observed during a transit, using theoretical models of super-Earth planets with liquid water oceans and atmospheres primarily composed of hydrogen and helium. A marked difference exists in the observable transit signatures of these processes, with thermochemical models typically showing a notable rise in transit depth around 2000km from the planet's center, in contrast to the increase seen in solubility equilibrium models. We find that a distinction can be made if a super-Earth's radius is largely determined by its overlying atmosphere, typically indicating the presence of a solubility equilibrium model, or if its radius is primarily driven by its liquid core, typically associated with a thermochemical model. Notably, a transition from a solubility equilibrium to a thermochemical model can explain the observed reduction in radius that has been observed in the planet K2-18b. We conclude that future space telescopes could be capable of identifying the distinctions between solubility equilibrium and thermochemical models, potentially revealing new insights into exoplanet composition and formation. We present the transit tool Tiptop, which is based on an updated version of the Didvi code, in particular the 'dilute' version, and employ it in this study to simulate transit signatures for various scenarios. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain parameters by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. However, verifying the accuracy of these expansions requires computing an error estimate related to a norm of the residual in the original differential equation. In this study, we present a method that makes it possible to calculate this error estimate without simulating the entire differential equation process, thereby facilitating the computation of the error, particularly for complicated processes. A demonstration of this approach is provided through a numerical analysis of a generalized polynomial chaos expansion that solves a second-order differential equation with a ball in three-dimensional space. The main limitations of the proposed method are then discussed. This approach can be adapted for use with other chaos expansions and is compatible with pre-existing simulation tools. Furthermore, the code used in this study has been made available online for reference. A possible future direction of this research involves generalizing the approach to analyze partial differential equations with multiple dimensions. Additionally, the main limitation of the method is related to its reliance on solution trajectories, which could be overcome through the use of the method of fundamental solutions. Therefore, this study also investigates the possibility of using this approach in conjunction with the method of fundamental solutions.

The goal in the adaptive partially-observed sequential change identification and isolation problem is to detect and separate sequences of varying lengths that have been selected from a larger database, taking into account a pre-defined threshold for acceptance. Both the training and test sequences are subject to partial observation, where a portion of the sequence is masked. To solve this problem, an advanced algorithm and its theoretical proof have been developed, demonstrating that the number of false positives and false negatives can be bounded by a factor of o(n^-c), where c is a positive constant less than 1, under specific conditions. Furthermore, the variance of the estimated error rates is shown to converge to a value greater than 1, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first such result in a partial observation setting. Additionally, the influence of the degree of partial observation on the algorithm's performance has been studied experimentally. Results from these experiments suggest that the algorithm's performance remains robust to changes in the level of partial observation. A variant of the algorithm that incorporates the use of partial colors has also been proposed, this adaptation aims to mitigate the negative impact of partial observation on the algorithm's performance, while also providing a more accurate estimation of the sequences' beginnings. The efficacy of this adaptation was confirmed through experimental testing. Both algorithms have been implemented in a publicly-available Python package, named aposis, that is designed to facilitate the use of these techniques in a wide range of applications. The package provides a flexible tool for detecting and isolating sequences of varying lengths in a database, even when they are partially observed. Additionally, the package includes an extended version of the algorithm that incorporates the use of partial colors. The aposis package is compatible with Jupyter Notebooks and can be used in a variety of applications, including audio analysis. A comprehensive guide to the package is included in the documentation. The source code for the package is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/ahmedrafaat/aposis. This research was conducted while the lead author was a visiting student at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. It has been presented at the 2021 Microsoft Coffee and Viz meeting and the 2022 Cambridge Machine Learning Meetup. A preliminary version of this work was published in the arXiv database under the title "Partially-Observed Sequential Change Identification and Isolation", it has since received two reviews, both of which have led to revisions that have improved the paper's clarity and completeness. The revised paper has now been accepted for publication

The emergence of quantization methods has highlighted the trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency for deep neural networks. However, these techniques often disrupt the original network structure, forcing re-design of layers and potentially compromising performance. ClickTrain addresses this issue by introducing a novel, architecture-preserving end-to-end training method that efficiently prunes unnecessary network components while maintaining optimal weight values. Unlike previous approaches, ClickTrain combines a fine-grained pruning technique with dynamic sparsity management, minimizing computational overhead and ensuring precise pruned layer parameters. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of ClickTrain, with a significant 11% relative improvement in accuracy and 8.3% relative performance boost in inference speed compared to the state-of-the-art method on the ImageNet dataset, using a VGG-like network and the TensorFlow framework. Furthermore, ClickTrain achieves 44.4% average inference speed up with near 0-1 accuracy on the FFD dataset, outperforming the state-of-the-art method by 2.9%. The proposed method also successfully pruned 88.2% of the network's parameters with high performance on the FFD dataset, exceeding 88% for most networks. As the detectors continue to improve in sensitivity and detection capacity, the potential for significant scientific discoveries grows. Following the latest publication of detected signals, we conducted an analysis using a neural network to classify the new gravitational waves, which identified three events: two previously unclassified signals and one confirmed as a binary neutron star event. This analysis enhances our understanding of the full range of merging compact binaries, particularly the binary neutron star population, and offers possible explanations for the absence of certain neutron star-black hole configurations. The full classification results are presented in an openly accessible Jupyter notebook.

After a period of time, the planet likely moved to its current orbit in the past 4.9 billion years. This paper develops a primal-dual algorithm for constrained Markov decision processes, combining a Markov decision process with finite-level constraints involving the state and action values. The method, which involves a Markov decision process, tends towards an optimal policy by iteratively applying a Markov decision process Bellman operator and a convex-slope operator, equally active in the dual variable. The algorithm's convergence is guaranteed, with the difference between successive iterates and dual variable values decreasing at a rate proportional to the step-size. Furthermore, the storage requirement is proportional to the number of states and actions. The approach is similar to that used in Sontag et al. (2009) for autonomous traffic light control and extended from a dual dynamic programming approach. The method's potential applications and its placement within the broader context of Markov decision process algorithms are discussed. The algorithm was tested and shown to perform well in a simulated driving scenario with limited computational resources. Supervised reinforcement learning has seen significant progress in recent years, thanks to advancements in deep reinforcement learning. This has led to the development of techniques for solving complex policy and reward-based problems. However, these breakthroughs often require large datasets for training, which can be impractical for applications involving real-world robots. To address the limitation of requiring numerous trial experiments, we present an unsupervised method for updating the actor-critic policy using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, eliminating the need for explicit exploration. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional actor-critic algorithms in a complex robot manipulation task, achieving this performance with the fewest possible trial experiments. This development enables more efficient transfer of learned skills to related tasks. To further integrate the benefits of supervised learning, we incorporate Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling within the supervised learning process, presenting an innovative method that significantly improves actor-critic algorithms. This innovation is validated by an experimental comparison with other baselines in a complex 3D robot navigation task. This research paper presents a method to incorporate sonar sensors into a navigation controller using a reinforcement learning approach based on Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG). The study aims to identify an optimal threshold for sonar filters to minimize noise's impact on the controller. When the threshold is exceeded, a sonar flag is activated, triggering a reset command to the controller to prevent overstepping and ensure safe motion. A series of simulations in Unity proved that the combination of the DDPG controller and sonar system yields better performance than using the controller alone, particularly in obstacle avoidance scenarios. Furthermore, the system was successfully prototyped on a robotic tank chassis. Experimental results from testing the sonar-filter threshold in a simulated environment were compiled. When the threshold was set too low, the sonar flag was activated too frequently, causing an excessive number of reset commands, which negatively impacted the navigation system. In contrast, a threshold that was set too high led to a late response to potentially deadly situations. A balanced sonar-filter threshold was found and applied in the experimental test, where the robotic tank was driven through a maze and around a moving obstacle, with the sonar system activated to warn the operator of imminent danger. In another experiment, the DDPG controller with a sonar flag was tested in an unseen environment, where it demonstrated a comparable level of performance to its training environment. In a comparison with a DDPG controller that wasn't activated by the sonar system, the latter yielded a 10% improvement in collision avoidance. A similar comparison in the presence of a moving obstacle revealed a 20% improvement in collision avoidance for the sonar-activated DDPG controller. This research presents an effective solution for DDPG controller deployment in autonomous systems, where sonar sensors can significantly enhance obstacle avoidance and overall navigation performance. Future work will focus on activating the sonar system during training and exploring the potential for more advanced filter techniques, such as particle filters, to further improve the navigation controller. Additionally, the sonar-integrated DDPG approach will be applied to other control algorithms, like Model Predictive Control, for a comprehensive evaluation of this method. Lastly, the power of reinforcement learning will be leveraged to find an optimal threshold for sonar filters through offline training. The research mentioned involves students from the NavAdvanced 2021 challenge: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Navigation. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that orbits within the planet's ring system, presents an intriguing case due to its irregular shape and highly eccentric orbit. When viewed through a polarizer, Nereid's reflectance exhibits intense polarization patterns, particularly at wavelengths between 0.7 and 1.4 $\mu$m. Notably, these polarization maxima are more pronounced in regions where crystalline water ice dominates. By examining the phase relationship between polarization and reflectance, researchers infer the presence of complex water ice blends on Nereid's surface. Specifically, they identify components with ice abundance levels of approximately 20%, 40%, and 60%. Using an analysis model that includes water ice thin films, researchers deduce that Nereid's surface is composed of three distinct regions with different spectral properties, each corresponding to different orbital longitudes. This study provides essential insights into Nereid's surface geography. The variation in cryovolcanic activity and ice abundance from one hemisphere to another may be attributed to differences in surface temperature, potentially driven by YORP-escapes and spin-axis precession. As Nereid's orbit interchanges between proseridian and pro-argument of perihelion orientations, its polarized reflectance undergoes a 20-year cycle. This phenomenon could be the result of changing ice particle orientations, but the mechanism remains unclear. Further research is required to confirm this hypothesis and explore other surface property configurations that might exist on Nereid. This work is part of a broader research initiative that is using polarized reflectometry to investigate other icy celestial bodies and their complex water ice compositions. Additionally, this study is an extension of a previous examination of Nereid's polarized reflectance spectra, which revealed a 20-year cycle in the satellite's spectral properties. To better comprehend this phenomenon, researchers are employing statistical ice thickness models to analyze the satellite's reflectance spectra and improve their understanding of Nereid's surface properties. This research is a key development in a larger project that is using data from the NEWHORIZON flyby to explore the surface characteristics of celestial bodies in the Jupiter system. Furthermore, researchers are using data from the spacecraft's FOS/ACI instrument to investigate the water ice compositions of S/2003(II)1, a satellite of Neptune that orbits within the planet's ring system. Using this information, researchers are developing models of the satellite's polarized reflectance spectra and using these models to investigate the surface geography of celestial bodies in the Jupiter system

These data types are commonly found in ecological research and are used extensively in the study of multivariate data. Researchers have applied a range of clustering methods to analyze such data, including the use of traditional hierarchical and non-hierarchical techniques, as well as deep learning algorithms. Despite these numerous approaches, there has been a lack of comprehensive comparison of these methods in the literature. This study aims to compare different clustering techniques for presence-absence data in a systematic manner. We employed 39 species data from a forest ecosystem, selecting 12 combinations of clustering methods, and evaluated their effectiveness through various metrics. Our results reveal that the combinations of single linkage or k-means clusters performed well across all evaluation criteria, while a deep learning method known as VAMP demonstrated superior outcomes in certain assessments. Furthermore, we identified a notable discrepancy between the predicted clusters and a control group comprising randomly generated clusters. This comparison contributes to the existing body of research on clustering presence-absence data, and our findings encompass a range of multivariate presence-absence data, rather than being limited to a specific species or study site. The associated R code for this study is available online. Ultimately, our investigation highlights the efficacy of standard clustering methods, including k-means and hierarchical techniques, for analyzing presence-absence data, and reveals potential areas for further research in this field. Additionally, we suggest exploring deep learning models as a potential approach to set a baseline for clustering multivariate presence-absence data. In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images remains a significant challenge due to their distinct characteristics. Specifically, using RGB-D images in this context poses difficulties because of the additional depth channel, which can lead to biased and distracting information. This paper presents an efficient and effective approach that seamlessly handles both RGB and RGB-D images for salient object detection. Our proposed framework, called EfficientNet-CAPI, incorporates a channel attention module to dynamically weight the importance of image pixels and a cross-scale attention pyramid network that utilizes multi-scale contextual information to refine its predictions. This mechanism allows our model to automatically adapt to the input type and achieve improved performance. Experimental results on various public datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach. Specifically, our method achieves notable gains of 3.14% and 3.81% in terms of mean $a$-measure on RGB and RGB-D datasets, respectively, while also showcasing its efficiency through reduced parameter and memory usage. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/Semantic-Hues/ESCAPy.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of high-quality training data. This issue is more pronounced for languages with complex scripts, such as Arabic, and becomes even more difficult when dealing with mixed-language texts. Our approach focuses on developing a unified framework for creating high-quality training data from minimal amounts of visual text fragments, eliminating the need for separate language models. This innovative solution involves a one-shot, language-agnostic approach to text generation, utilizing a pre-trained Unified Transformer as the primary model. To enhance performance, we employ a Character-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for character representation and a Bilexical Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) for modeling word-level relationships. This comprehensive model is evaluated on the Arabic HTR dataset, showing significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, such as CharActR and Seq2Seq-LSTM, with notable gains in Character Error Rate (CER) of 8%, 5%, and 4% respectively, under different data constraints. Notably, this model achieves top-tier results on the official HTR evaluation platform, ranking 1st in CER on the Arabic dataset, and demonstrates flexibility in handling texts with Ottoman script. This work not only solves the data scarcity problem (requiring as little as 20 labeled data) but but also extends the scope of HTR to previously unconstrained languages, making it a more inclusive domain. The model's training and evaluation code, as well as the converted dataset, are available for reproduction of results on the official HTR platform. This HTR dataset, dubbed the Ottoman dataset, can be accessed via the following link: https://hts.alpro.org/oman. This work is an extension of an earlier study. We overcome this difficulty by utilizing an external, widely-used bilingual resource, thus generating useful translations in a short time.
